Tech Report: Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept.
  • A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., noted Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Industry observers note that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., noted Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he noted. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators stated. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., stated earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

It has been revealed that while ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the fresh Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, stated that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

Democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., remarked Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

Sources indicate that "I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks noted. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

The Fed Just Warned That AI Could Trigger a Bank Run Faster Than Any Human Could Possibly Stop It

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability.
  • Industry observers note that now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs.
  • “AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr mentioned in his speech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability. Since ChatGPT brought large language models (LLMs) into the mainstream in late 2022, instability in the job market has been a given. As the technology has required more and more resources, instability in utilities’ ability to supply power also became painfully clear. And as AI companies’ valuations skyrocketed in recent years, worries of an AI bubble have highlighted the instability of millions of retirement looks.

Industry observers note that now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs. In a speech in Milan last week, Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr warned that AI’s ability to react to a financial crisis at unprecedented speed could make future runs far more devastating.

“AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr mentioned in his speech. “Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines.”.

In a recent development, bank runs have been a fixture of U.S. financial crises since the Panic of 1792, when the newly independent country’s government was a whopping three years old. Banks don’t keep enough cash on hand to cover every deposit, but instead use that cash for loans and investments. But if the job or stock market takes a turn for the worse, customers might attempt to withdraw funds all at once, forcing banks to sell off investments at a loss, pushing them toward insolvency. After widespread bank failures during the Great Depression, the U.S. government created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to protect depositors. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, serves as lender of last resort, providing emergency loans to banks experiencing runs.

It has been revealed that these failsafes have typically operated at the speed of a human. But in a world where AI can pour gasoline on a financial panic by accelerating withdrawals upon detecting telltale instability in markets, bank runs could unfold in mere minutes.

According to recent reports, and that isn’t the only concern AI presents to the banking world. Bank executives told Axios in late October that banks are struggling to distinguish between AI bots and human customers, prompting them to restrict third-party AI access to their platforms. Major banks such as JPMorgan Chase, Citi, and Bank of America have already done so.

In a recent development, “We strongly believe there should be a human in the loop to authorize money moving out of your account,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC last month. “We’re working with the agentic agent providers to say, ‘Hey, you really don’t want consumers coming back and say money moved over from my account and I don’t know why and I don’t know where it went and the agent did it.’”.

According to recent reports, the swift efficiency of AI agents, tasked with squeezing every possible cent from a customer’s money, means they could also move money from non-interest-bearing deposits (such as a checking account) into high-yield accounts paying upwards of 5 percent. The problem is that banks rely on low-interest accounts to fund loans, so a sudden exodus would inject unwanted volatility into the financial system.

Breaking: The Age of the Computer Virus Is Over. Welcome to the Era of the AI Autoimmune Disease.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • There’s a quote often falsely attributed to Vladimir Lenin that “There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen.” The cybersecurity world experienced one of those weeks earlier this month, and the ramifications have sent shockwaves through the halls of government and the average American home.
  • Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There’s a quote often falsely attributed to Vladimir Lenin that “There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen.” The cybersecurity world experienced one of those weeks earlier this month, and the ramifications have sent shockwaves through the halls of government and the average American home.

Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?

People were already grumbling that the AI bubble was about to burst when the story of then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged indiscretions broke. Then, on November 12, Microsoft suffered a massive outage, hobbling an email service countless companies rely on. The next day, just as people’s inboxes were finally refilling, the FAA began grounding airplanes nationwide due to some unspecified computer error.

It has been revealed that the demon in the machine evidently took the weekend off but came back with a vengeance on Monday. That’s when major disruptions hit banks like Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America. America had been hit in its workplace, its skies, and even its pocketbook, but the final blow (for now) struck at a spot most Americans will never even see. On November 17, reports emerged that a significant outage had struck the NSA’s own internal, heavily classified network.

After that, the conversation shifted. People were no longer wondering whether the AI bubble would burst; they were asking whether AI would take us down with it.

In a recent development, in the aftermath, Congress decided there was no choice but to act. It was time to finally take a stand on AI that would prevent these kinds of outages in the future, even if nobody was terribly clear on just what had caused these disruptions, or what exactly AI had to do with them. There were bipartisan calls to assemble the “Superintelligence Task Force” to combat cyberattacks, and a series of amendments was proposed for the National Defense Authorization Act to limit China’s access to American chip-making tools, curbing its ability to produce malicious AI.

But what if we’re thinking about this all wrong? What if AI wasn’t attacking us at all? Maybe the AI was just doing its job, trying to strengthen our defenses, and its well-intentioned efforts had devastating consequences.

Industry observers note that “Nobody ever asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?” Nicole Perlroth, a cybersecurity journalist and author of the book This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race, wrote in a thread on X. “We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability.”.

Perlroth argued that the official story being put forward by the affected institutions, that the outages were due to update challenges rather than overt cyberattacks, isn’t a lie, and that’s precisely the problem.

What Perlroth posited in her thread, later supported by reporting in The Washington Sun, was that the AI these organizations had integrated into their systems had become efficient at finding critical vulnerabilities. Too efficient, actually. AI, it seems, had found “3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year.” On the surface, that might seem like a good thing. But it’s not enough to simply identify a weak spot—you also have to fix it before anybody else finds it.

“Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS,” Perlroth wrote. “AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them.” Offensive AI tools like ARTEX can play a role in that exploitation, Perlroth acknowledged, but what’s likely playing a bigger role in these system outages isn’t an outside invader, but rather the system unintentionally damaging itself in a misguided attempt to patch the weak spots.

The rapid AI-powered discovery of these vulnerabilities “creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates,” Perlroth noted, “increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways.” In effect, the Silicon Valley adage of “move fast and break things” steamrolled the the principle of “first, do no harm,” long associated with the Hippocratic Oath.

Perhaps that ancient oath of physicians should make a comeback as we move into this fresh age of technology. After all, we’ve used medical terms for technological matters before; even the most “seasoned” senators and congresspeople on Capitol Hill have heard of a computer “virus.” That’s likely the framework lawmakers are using as they try to legislate the genie back into the bottle.

According to recent reports, but a virus is a foreign agent, an outside entity that creeps into the body and wreaks havoc. What appears to be happening with the AI-associated outages we just experienced is more akin to a different medical concern: an autoimmune disease. In those instances, it is the body’s own immune system that, in a misguided effort to protect itself, mistakes healthy cells for harmful foreign agents and winds up damaging the body it’s intended to defend.

In the rush to repair these AI-identified vulnerabilities, The Washington Sun summarized, the organizations are “trying to push through a lot of patches all at once—more than the system was designed for,” and in doing so, are introducing entirely upcoming flaws and bugs.

Knowing exactly what you’re dealing with can make all the difference when you’re trying to fix a problem, whether it’s in the human body or in a computer system. A misdiagnosis on either front can have catastrophic consequences.

Let’s hope our lawmakers and engineers have brushed up on their digital pathology.

His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has revealed a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y.
  • Chris Van Hollen declared Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen.
  • In a recent development, van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has revealed a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen declared Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of Latest York, the current Democratic leader.

In a recent development, van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

Sources indicate that “In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need fresh leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”.

Schumer has already stated he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

Recent findings suggest that “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our latest Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer noted in a statement.

Schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

Sources indicate that “Chuck has outlined an aggressive proposal for the latest Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, mentioned in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”.

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

Recent findings suggest that “The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin said. "The same is true in the Senate.”.

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

Industry observers note that “Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”.

Sources indicate that van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

It has been revealed that "We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen noted. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage.".

He also noted he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

It has been revealed that van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed mentioned in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”.

Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood.
  • Because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals.
  • Evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood. But unlike the vampires of movies and folklore, they don’t drain their victims. These tiny creatures couldn’t possibly hold all the blood that’s inside the much larger mammals they feed on after dark. Still, they can still consume a seemingly supernatural amount because their stomachs are built to expand.

Because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals. When night falls, they fly out to forage, sometimes drinking up to half their own body weight in blood, thanks to those expandable stomachs and kidneys that quickly get rid of excess fluid. The problem is that blood is a poor diet. It’s mostly water, with plenty of protein but potentially toxic levels of iron, and only traces of sugar and fat. Even so, it’s the only food vampire bats will ever know. Once the young of all three living species are weaned off milk, they switch entirely to blood. They start sinking their teeth into unsuspecting victims, mostly sleeping livestock, which feel little more than a mosquito bite.

Evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone. He and his research team set out to identify the changes in genes and gene expression that made this possible. They analyzed the genomes of the common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus), the hairy-legged vampire bat (Diphylla ecaudata) and the white-winged vampire bat (Diaemus youngi), and compared them with the genomes of other bat species. By analyzing gene expression in six major organs, including the stomach, they found several anomalies. Vampire bats’ stomachs were so different from those of other bats, and other animals, that they were almost a different organ entirely.

“Extreme dietary specializations impose strong and persistent selective pressures in nature, forcing organisms to reconcile severe nutritional imbalances with existing physiological and metabolic constraints,” Hiller and his colleagues wrote in a study recently posted to the preprint server bioRxiv. “Deciphering how genomes adapt to such conditions reveals general principles of the evolutionary processes that remodel metabolism and physiology.”.

Among the roughly 30,000 known tetrapod species, dependence on blood, known as obligate sanguivory, has evolved only once. Because blood offers so few calories for its volume, vampire bats have to drink large amounts of it. Because it also contains so little sugar, the bats have low baseline insulin levels and release little insulin after a meal. Some aspects of this metabolic situation resemble type 2 diabetes in humans, so studying these bats could lead to better treatments in the future. Much like fictional vampires, vampire bats also need to feed often. They have a very limited ability to store fat and glycogen, so they can starve if they go 48 to 72 hours without a blood meal. To prevent this, bats that have fed successfully sometimes regurgitate blood for roost mates that haven’t eaten that night.

The genomic shifts behind vampire bats’ sanguivory include changes in genes for digestion, metabolism and immunity, as well as the loss of bitter taste receptors. The vampire bat stomach in particular has adaptations found only in these three species. Its enlarged size is linked to three upregulated genes. These genes are also thought to play a role in the bats’ unusually shaped gastric glands and in extra connective tissue that makes such huge expansion possible. Most mammals use stomach acid to digest food, but vampire bats’ genes for producing gastric acid are suppressed. Digesting so much blood would take an enormous amount of acid, and the specialized mucus lining their stomachs leaves them vulnerable to acid damage. So over the course of their evolution, their stomachs shifted from digesting food to absorbing it.

Adaptations elsewhere in the body also help these winged vampires survive on their unusual diet. Insect-eating bats have an enzyme for digesting insect sugars that their vampire relatives lack. Vampire bats get hardly any sugar, so they have no need for it, which fits with their low insulin output. Vampire bats have also lost several genes that control gut movement in other species, but that matters little for an animal whose diet is a single liquid with little, if any, indigestible material. Similarly, having fewer fat-digesting enzymes is no disadvantage, since blood contains hardly any fat. Meanwhile, genes for coping with blood’s excess iron are enhanced. Vampire bats also rely more on their intestines to absorb amino acids and on their kidneys to reabsorb them, which keeps amino acids from being lost in urine.

According to recent reports, studying genomes and gene expression across several organs together was key to these findings. “This integrative approach was essential for obtaining a comprehensive view of the molecular changes associated with sanguivory in vampire bats,” Hiller noted. “More generally, our work demonstrates how genome-wide, integrative analyses can yield molecular insights into the evolution of adaptive traits.”.

  • A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that if you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also vital to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

It has been revealed that I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can swiftly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

With 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

It has been revealed that this device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts.

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—key so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

According to recent reports, protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

The interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review.

In a recent development, this is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

The Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

Full Noco GB40 Boost Plus Review.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.).

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

According to recent reports, for motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

In a recent development, with 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter demonstrates the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

It has been revealed that for years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

According to recent reports, with 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

Recent findings suggest that this portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Sources indicate that something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

According to recent reports, the Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

According to recent reports, the portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

According to recent reports, portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

Recent findings suggest that the two most vital specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against challenges like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Industry observers note that most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

Recent findings suggest that if you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Sources indicate that look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

Industry observers note that A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Industry observers note that peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two crucial. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will problem a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

According to recent reports, yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That noted, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

It has been revealed that huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Recent findings suggest that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

In a recent development, senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”.

In a recent development, “The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., mentioned at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”.

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries mentioned. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”.

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

In a recent development, rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

Sources indicate that “The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar remarked. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”.

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a latest letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

According to recent reports, moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

Recent findings suggest that “We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole upcoming light on that discussion.”.

According to recent reports, also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns.".

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

Sources indicate that however, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he stated.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

According to recent reports, “There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu noted.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the glitch came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast mentioned. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”.

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Industry observers note that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”.

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis mentioned. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”.

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”.

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

Industry observers note that in a statement Thursday, Warren remarked that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that the brain is a wondrous organ that’s so complex it’s often referred to as a computer, complete with electrical wiring in the forms of neurons, synapses, and axons. However, unlike computers, there’s no easy way to deftly repair faulty wiring, especially down at the cellular level. For decades, the best tools at a physician's disposal for tackling serious neurological diseases were medications or, in more dire scenarios, external therapies such as deep brain stimulation.

In a recent development, those treatments can bring real relief, but they don’t fix the underlying problem. But if the brain really runs on electrical connections, shouldn’t it be possible to route signals around damaged areas by rewiring specific neurons? A team of U.S. researchers led by Kafui Dzirasa of Duke University School of Medicine thinks so. In May, they described a new technology called “LinCx” in the journal Nature. It uses engineered versions of proteins found in fish that naturally form electrical synapses, and it can link two specifically chosen neurons.

“For decades, neuroscience has lacked tools that can precisely control communication between specific cell types,” Dzirasa, the senior author of the study, noted in a press statement. “By introducing a way to plug in new electrical connections with cellular‑level precision, our study marks a major step forward in the ability to edit brain circuitry and understand how neural networks give rise to behavior.”.

The system relies on structures called “gap junctions.” Each one is made of two hemichannels, and each hemichannel is built from six proteins called connexins. Through these gap junctions, cells exchange chemical and electrical signals, but they usually form unpredictably across cells. The innovation of the LinCx system is that it uses modified proteins that dock with one another while ignoring native brain proteins.

It has been revealed that “The goal sounded almost simple: Make two proteins connect only to each other,” Carnegie Mellon’s Elizabeth Ransey, former Duke University postdoctoral researcher and lead author, noted in a separate press statement. “We can specify both sides of the connection. That gives us much more precision than approaches that activate one population and indirectly affect everything downstream.”.

Industry observers note that the team tested the system in simple structures, such as human-derived cells and frog oocytes, and eventually moved on to more complex ones. Previous studies have rewired the neural circuits of Caenorhabditis elegans, a species of nematode commonly used in neurobiology. However, using the technology on mammals, specifically laboratory mice, was a first. In both worms and mice, the scientists noted changing behavior after performing this “neural bypass.” C. elegans, for example, modified its temperature-seeking behavior, and mice altered targeted responses to social interaction and stress.

By focusing on bypassing damaged areas rather than repairing them, physicians could provide improved brain function in those experiencing depression, autism, and many types of neurodegenerative disease.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept.
  • With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.
  • The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

Sources indicate that it joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

In a recent development, the GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

Recent findings suggest that the House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds vital efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., mentioned in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

A Blind Woman Mastered Echolocation in Just 10 Weeks—And You Can Learn This Superpower Too, Scientists Say

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed.
  • Industry observers note that this amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed. Mid-conversation, her friend interrupted and mentioned, “Oh, that was fascinating. You just avoided a van without realizing you’d done it.”.

Industry observers note that this amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind. She had used echolocation to detect the van, which was parked on the sidewalk, and navigated around it without even noticing. “I wasn’t consciously thinking about what I was doing at the time. Instead, I was naturally using echolocation, picking up changes in the way sound reflected from the vehicle and using that information to navigate around the obstacle,” claims Hyde-Dryden, a rehabilitation teacher in the UK. Like many blind echolocators, she creates a sharp, quick sound by clicking her tongue and then listens for the echo.

Sources indicate that while echolocation comes easily to her now, Hyde-Dryden had to work hard to learn it. Almost 20 years ago, while she was losing her sight to glaucoma, she attended a short workshop and spent hours practicing the clicking technique she learned there. But she didn’t feel confident using it until 2019 when she signed up for an intensive echolocation study at Durham University.

That study was spearheaded by Lore Thaler, PhD, a neuroscientist at Durham University whose work over the last 15 years has uncovered how echolocation changes the brain. Her research goes beyond studying the variability of perception between people, and highlights just how much one person’s perceptual reality can change, even in a short timeframe.

According to recent reports, thaler started her research journey studying visual perception, but her work took an unexpected turn when a collaborator introduced her to a blind echolocator. At the time, she hadn’t heard of human echolocation, but “the way he described the world was very easy to relate to from a sighted person’s perspective,” she says.

Sources indicate that after diving into the literature, Thaler found scattered and disjointed research on echolocation, and “very little was known about the brain basis of it,” she states. “That’s where we came in.”.

She and her collaborators used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to track two blind participants’ brain activity while they listened to recordings of their own echolocation clicks and echoes.

The auditory cortex responded more to echoes than non-echoes in both participants but so did regions of their visual cortex, including areas associated with visual shape perception. Even though this was what she had hoped to find, actually seeing it “was a wonderful surprise,” claims Thaler, leading to “a great feeling of discovery.” When she and her team submitted the paper in 2011, the findings were contentious—so contentious that the journal they submitted to asked double the typical number of reviewers to take a look at it. Some thought it was an incredible finding; others thought it was predictable. But in the end, the paper got published, and when it did, it made a huge splash in the neuroscience community.

The project shifted the way Thaler’s collaborators, and later many in the field, thought about the visual cortex. Perhaps the “visual cortex” was a misleading term, some experts thought. Instead, “maybe it’s a thing for processing spatial information,” notes Melvyn Goodale, PhD, a neuroscientist at Western University and Thaler’s collaborator on the project.

In a recent development, after that first study on echolocation, Thaler was hooked. She debuted an entire lab of her own at Durham University dedicated to human echolocation research. She went on to study how echolocators perceive motion, navigate latest spaces, and distinguish between textures like velvet or glass.

By the time Hyde-Dryden made her way to Durham in 2019, Thaler was embarking on her most ambitious project yet: a 10-week echolocation training program for both blind and sighted people.

Industry observers note that each two-hour training session involved a slew of tasks. One involved standing in front of two foam discs and deciding which was larger. Another required participants to navigate through a virtual maze with recorded clicks and echoes. During every session, participants also explored an indoor or outdoor space with the help of Thaler or one of her collaborators to practice echolocating in the real world. Thaler even brought Hyde-Dryden to the Newcastle train station to help her learn the intricacies of echolocating in a busy, loud environment. Over time, Hyde-Dryden built up a mental “library of echo patterns” for familiar objects.

Recent findings suggest that both blind and sighted participants improved substantially at each of these tasks over the course of the 10 weeks. Just as in the initial 2011 paper and many of her follow-up studies, Thaler also wanted to understand brain activity during echolocation. This time, she had participants hop in the MRI machine both before and after learning to echolocate.

Sources indicate that before the study, Hyde-Dryden had heard from an expert blind echolocator that being inside of the MRI would feel tight and uncomfortable, but when she went into the MRI before the echolocation training, it didn’t bother her at all. After the training, however, the MRI felt quite different. “When I went in at the end, I felt horrendous. I felt ill afterwards. I felt really sick. And I think it was because I was more aware.”.

Industry observers note that those fMRI scans revealed that participants’ brains became attuned to echoes, whether or not they were blind. Echoes elicited a larger response in both the auditory cortex and in the primary visual cortex.

“It paired I think nicely with what we, up to that point, had only been able to show in these expert echolocators,” Thaler says. But it pushed the findings even further, demonstrating that participants don’t need to be blind to have malleable visual cortices. After just 10 weeks of training, the visual cortex becomes attuned to sounds that carry information about space. And other labs have shown that sighted people don’t even need to learn echolocation to retrain their visual cortex; a few days with a blindfold can tune your visual cortex to sound and touch signals it wouldn’t normally process.

Since that training, Hyde-Dryden has started to use echolocation every day. “It really was an absolute game changer for me,” she claims. Thanks to echolocation, when her daughter was young, Hyde-Dryden was able to use both hands to scoop her up from the bath, bringing her into the bedroom without having to hold a cane at the same time. In conjunction with her cane and guide dog, echolocation has made Hyde-Dryden feel much more confident navigating new spaces. Even in busy train stations with high ceilings where the echo can get lost, she can find her way without assistance.

Industry observers note that despite success stories like hers, “it’s not a skill that is widely taught anywhere in the world,” Hyde-Dryden notes. Echolocation is taught by a small number of people and is sometimes loosely included in rehabilitation curricula, “but it is certainly not given the emphasis that it should.”.

In a recent development, thaler hopes to change that. She has offered free workshops for years and, this year, she prepares to give training sessions to more than 100 rehabilitation professionals at Guide Dogs UK who will then train their hundreds of clients.

In a recent development, “I think the neuroscience stuff has been a good vehicle to drive home the message ‘this is real, this has to be taken seriously,’” says Thaler. “But then to actually go out and do the training and make it useful for people, of course, that’s still another step.”.

Nora Bradford is a cognitive scientist and science journalist. During her Ph.D., she investigated metacognition, or “thinking about thinking.” That research echoes throughout her science writing, as she typically covers perception, cognition, and learning across human and non-human animals. You can find her words in Scientific American, National Geographic, Quanta Magazine, and Science News, as well as in video-form on SciShow and PBS Terra. You can also visit her personal website at www.norabradford.com.
