    #157117. Latest Update: How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1596 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions.
    • I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive.
    • It has been revealed that you could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions. Dilapidated, neglected neighborhoods share city space with splendid palaces and world-beating museums. The city’s origins go back to the ancient Greeks, yet the contemporary art scene here is buzzing. There is a state-of-the-art metro system designed by renowned artists and architects (no wonder, since the traffic is infamously heavy).

    I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive. Naples today is safer, more tourist-friendly, and cleaner than ever before, yet it remains Italy’s most beguiling city. The eating and drinking scene has evolved, there is a much wider choice of places to stay (with Rocco Forte due to open a hotel here in 2027), and museums and monuments have been spruced up and reorganized. In 2027, the America’s Cup will arrive as well.

    It has been revealed that you could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything. But if you only have three days, start early and be prepared to pack in as much as possible; you can rest once you get home. Here is my advice for how to make the most of it.

    You coudl easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything—but three days are a delicious taste, too.

    In a recent development, historic Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a perfect place to start your first day, shoulder to shoulder with the locals at the bar for a shot of espresso and a warm cornetto (only tourists sit on the terrace). Just across Piazza Trieste e Trento lies the imposing dark grey and red Palazzo Reale where you can visit the sumptuous Royal Apartments and ornate Teatrino, and on the other side is the Teatro San Carlo, one of Italy’s most prestigious opera houses; opera buffs can book a behind-the-scenes tour, or even better, tickets for a performance.

    From the Toledo metro station, you get full immersion in the Stazione d’Arte, a public art project involving some of the greatest contemporary artists and architects who have transformed Naples’ main underground stations into public galleries. Dominated by Oscar Tusquets Blanca’s jaw-dropping mosaic, Toledo is one of the most impressive—but for just the price of a metro ticket (just over $2), you can tour them all.

    A quick walk north on Via Toledo leads to Via della Pignasecca, where you can catch the end of the lively morning market with its troughs of slithering, glistening fish and seafood, piles of seasonal fruit and vegetables, and stalls selling everything from tripe to knock-off designer handbags.

    Lunch at no-nonsense Trattoria da Nenella near Piazza Carità is a noisy, fun experience; you’ll probably have to queue, but the deep-fried anchovies and meatballs in tomato sauce are worth it, and prices are rock-bottom.

    The Cappella Sansevero is home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    It has been revealed that after a shot of the best coffee in the city at Café Mexico in Piazza Dante, you can spend the afternoon exploring the grid of streets around the so-called Spaccanapoli, the heart of Roman Neapolis where ancient monuments rub shoulders with street food stalls, tiny grocers, once-grand palazzi, and shops selling tourist trinkets and religious memorabilia. Piazza del Gesù, at the western end, is dominated by the eponymous church and an ornate roccoco ‘guglia’. Just to the east is the Church and Convent of Santa Chiara with a beautiful Gothic interior and a cloister famous for its bright, 18th-century majolica tiles. Close by is Naples’ most celebrated (and most crowded) sight, the Cappella Sansevero, home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    Back on the Spaccanapoli, nip into Gay-Odin (n. 61) for a chocolate gelato and then continue to the vast Duomo where you will be dazzled by the gilt-encrusted Cappella di San Gennaro and the subterranean church of Santa Restituita and its 4th-century baptistery.

    Close by are the chapel of Pio Monte della Misericordia with Caravaggio’s seminal Seven Acts of Mercy and crumbling Piazza San Girolamini where Banksy’s Madonna with a Pistol appeared on the back right-hand wall in 2004. San Lorenzo Maggiore is an essential visit if you want to understand multi-layered Naples; under the 13th-century church, ongoing excavations have revealed the astonishing remains of a Greco-Roman city dating back 2,000 years.

    A detour down Via San Gregorio Armeno takes you past shops selling pastori or figurines for Christmas cribs. Much of what you see is mass-produced these days, so for the real deal, visit Marco Ferrigno’s workshop at number 10. Continue to leafy Piazza Bellini, a lively evening hub, and bag a terrace table at Café Intramoenia for a Campari spritz—you’ve earned it.

    For dinner, Europeo di Mattozzi is a personal favorite for its echoes of elegant old Naples; the classic food is fantastic (try the sublime melanzane alla parmigiana and the pasta with potatoes and provola cheese), the host Alfonso is charming, and your fellow diners are likely to be mostly locals.

    Use Castel dell'Ovoa as your launchpad for a classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag.

    Day two starts where it all began. Parthenope—later Neapolis and later still Napoli—was founded more than 2,500 years ago on the tiny island of Megaris, now occupied by the Castel dell’Ovo and the picturesque fishing hamlet of Borgo Marinari. There’s nothing much to see in the castle, but it’s a good launch pad for the classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag. It’s lined with restaurants and cafés offering tables in the sun for a cappuccino and magnificent views.

    It has been revealed that the delightful neighbourhood of Chiaia is a criss-cross of pretty cobbled lanes peppered with independent boutiques, cool bars, and tiny restaurants; Via dei Mille and Via dei Filangeri are known for designer clothes and chic galleries. The handmade silk ties at tiny, old-fashioned Marinella make wonderful gifts, and a counter perch at tiny Pescheria Mattiucci is a good choice for a quick seafood lunch with a glass of something chilled and white.

    Depending on the weather (and energy levels), one option from here is to head west beyond Mergellina to the upmarket seaside suburb of Posillipo for an afternoon on the beach; sunbeds and umbrellas can be rented at Bagno Sirena.

    Recent findings suggest that or you can hop on the Funicolare di Chiaia and trundle up to leafy Vomero and the panoramic Certosa di San Martino, a Carthusian monastery complex with an ornate church, several museums, two cloisters, and the famous Monk’s Cemetery decorated with marble skulls. It also has knock-out views over the whole waterfront and the Bay of Naples to the Sorrentine Peninsula. The Friggitoria Vomero—one of the city’s few remaining authentic ‘frying shops’—doles out sizzling snacks from 6 p.m. and is conveniently close to the funicolare stop as you head back down the hill.

    Chiaia’s quiet lanes morph into a nightlife hub from aperitivo hour on, filling up with smartly dressed locals and visitors in search of a good night out. Cocktail spot per eccellenza is retro-glam Antiquario where the jacketed barmen mix a stonking Negroni. From here it’s a short stroll to tiny Ristorante Dora, open since 1973, for textbook versions of fish and seafood classics such as spaghetti alle vongole (with local clams). Head back to Chiaia for a nightcap; follow your nose and the party crowd.

    The atmospheric burial site of Cimitero delle Fontanelle is a respite from the buzzing streets above.

    A no-go area for tourists until relatively recently, the dilapidated, densely populated but intriguing Rione Sanità is Naples in the raw. Breakfast at Pasticceria Popella in Via Arena alla Sanità is a must for their sfogliatelle and cream-stuffed ‘fiocchi di neve’ before having a rummage among the market stalls and tiny shops on Via dei Vergini; at n. 19 is the grand entrance to the famous pale green and cream Palazzo dello Spagnuolo with its celebrated ‘flying staircase’ by local architect Ferdinando San Felice.

    These shambolic streets are filled with tooting cars, buzzing vespas, and bewildered tourists, but there are hidden artistic gems too: the 2,400 year-old recently restored Ipogeo dei Cristallini, the atmospheric burial site of the Cimitero delle Fontanelle with its piles of skulls and bones; and the labyrinthine Catacombs of San Gaudioso under the basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità.

    You can’t visit the Sanità without a meal at Ciro Oliva’s crazy-lively temple to pizza Concettina ai Tre Santi (booking is essential), where the tasting menus offer an endless succession of slices topped with whatever the pizzaiolo dreams up at the time.

    Naples’ Archaeological Museum (aka Mann) houses one of the world’s great collections of ancient art and artefacts, and if you only visit one museum, make it this. Must-sees include the monumental Roman sculptures on the ground floor, the collection of ancient erotica in the Gabinetto Segreto, and the dazzling mosaics, wall paintings, and bronzes from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

    Afterwards, check out the brilliant selection of exquisite handmade gloves at factory prices in the workshops of Omega, a family glove business that first opened in 1923, before winding up the day in the surprisingly peaceful oasis of the exotic Orto Botanico gardens on traffic-clogged Via Foria.

    In a recent development, for a last blast, Grand Hotel Parker’s on the way up to Vomero is the smart place to go. Cocktails and light bites are served on the rooftop terrace while on the floor below, chef Domenico Candela whips up a storm with his two-Michelin-star take on local cuisine to a backdrop of unforgettable views.

    Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    Industry observers note that “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries noted, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Massive Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    In a recent development, on healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust upcoming majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The Newly introduced York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Without an unveiled challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    According to recent reports, rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries mentioned Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    It has been revealed that this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that believe it or not, Thanksgiving is around the corner. Families around the country are working on their grocery lists — and maybe keeping an eye on the wild shopping days that come after we dine with family and friends. If you're hoping to snag some great travel deals for Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday, TPG has a dedicated page where you can find our favorite deals.

    And if you need a little inspiration for your next vacation, we just released our annual Where to Go list for 2027. This year's list ranges from Texas Hill Country to Tunisia and from the Cayman Islands to Kazakhstan.

    Now, here's the hotel news you need to know about from this week.

    Hyatt is expanding its lifestyle footprint with the opening of the first Andaz in Australia. The Andaz Gold Coast, located in sunny Queensland, will have 202 rooms and plans to "redefine coastal luxury through a distinctive blend of expressive Australian design and immersive experiences inspired by the people, places, and creative spirit of the Gold Coast," according to a statement from Hyatt. The property is near the beaches of Broadbeach, and features a series of bars and restaurants, plus a lively pool club offering live music and community-focused barbecues.

    Also in Queensland, Brisbane will welcome a Park Hyatt in 2031, ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. Brisbane is one of my favorite cities, so I can't wait (though I'll have to) for the 201-room property not far from Suncorp Stadium, which will host a series of soccer and rugby events. Many details about the property are still under wraps, but if it's even half as great as the Park Hyatt Sydney, we know it'll be a great hotel.

    If you haven't had the chance to visit Houston, I can't recommend it enough. The city is home to diverse cultures, incredible food and the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo, one of the biggest rodeos in the world. If you find yourself in Beyoncé's hometown, consider a stay at the JW Marriott Houston Downtown, which just completed a years-long head-to-toe remodel. The hotel now features fresh rooms, including 56 newly introduced rooms, a redesigned lobby restaurant and a total revamp of the hotel's food and beverage offerings.

    Monti, my favorite neighborhood in Rome, feels like stepping back in time. Or, at least into a movie set, thanks to its beautiful vine-covered walls, cobblestone streets and lively energy near the Colosseum. In 2028, it'll also be home to Hortus Monti Rome, part of Hilton's upscale LXR Hotels & Resorts. The hotel is spread across six historic Umbertine-era buildings, according to a statement from Hilton and features a central garden, a spa, bars and restaurants and more.

    Until then, Hilton fans should check into Rome Cavalieri, one of the most popular Waldorf Astoria hotels in the world.

    Sources indicate that the Coke versus Pepsi debate is a serious one, and people tend to have strong opinions about which is better. While I'm a Diet Dr. Pepper fanatic myself, it looks like Hyatt is doubling down on its relationship with Pepsi. The manufacturer just renewed its contract, making PepsiCo the preferred beverage partner across 700 Hyatt properties in the United States. The agreement also extends to certain PepsiCo snack products.

    Earlier this year, Marriott ousted Pepsi and made Coca-Cola its "global beverage partner across several categories, including carbonated soft drinks and a growing range of hydration and functional beverages.".

    This $13 Cheese Plate Is One Thing American Airlines Gets Right

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A cheese tray is hardly the most exciting thing you can order on an airplane, but American Airlines does this one very well.
    • American sells its fruit and cheese plate for $13 or 1,300 AAdvantage miles (please folks, don’t use miles to pay for it).
    • I loved all three varieties of cheese (I’m not fan of bleu or brie, so very happy not to have to waste anything).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A cheese tray is hardly the most exciting thing you can order on an airplane, but American Airlines does this one very well. I recently enjoyed its buy-on-board fruit and cheese plate in economy class and would choose it over the comparable offerings on Delta or United. Let’s take a closer look in this week’s Meal of the Week.

    American sells its fruit and cheese plate for $13 or 1,300 AAdvantage miles (please folks, don’t use miles to pay for it). The current selection includes:.

    I loved all three varieties of cheese (I’m not fan of bleu or brie, so very happy not to have to waste anything).

    The crackers were excellent too. That might sound like a minor detail, but good cheese deserves good crackers, and these complemented the cheese very well…oh how I loathe soda crackers.

    The apples were sweet and crisp, I enjoyed the single fig, and I loved finishing with the Toblerone. A little chocolate at the end was just right…that’s often my dessert at home too.

    I have enjoyed cheese plates on Delta and United too, but American offers the superior economy class version, in my opinion. I really liked the blueberry artigiano and smoked black pepper cheddar.

    This was a late evening flight where I had planned to eat in the lounge before my flight but due to a flight delay jumped onto an earlier flight. It was 8:00 pm, I had not eaten, and had I been flying on United I would have been out of luck since you have to pre-order any food onboard beyond snack boxes.

    I figured I would have to make a Taco Bell run in LA when I landed, but this proved enough..and my body thanks me.

    American Airlines has a very good buy-on-board cheese plate. I enjoyed all three cheeses, the crackers were excellent, the apples were sweet, and the Toblerone was a nice dessert.

    Industry observers note that simple food can be very satisfying when the ingredients are good. This is something American does better than Delta or United in economy class, and I would gladly order it again.

    p.s. If you’re still feeling peckish, you might also enjoy a bag of salted, mixed nuts from Nuts & Clark…$11 or 1,100 miles. Also recommended!

    My Meal of the Week feature examines an airline meal from my travels over the years. This may be a meal from earlier in the week or it may be a meal served over a decade ago.

    #157112. American’s Longtime Chief Operating Officer to Retire

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (281 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Airlinegeeks ↗ Open Full Page

    American’s Longtime Chief Operating Officer to Retire

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (281 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.
    • 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.
    • Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.

    Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    It has been revealed that american will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A new reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be declared in December.

    Sources indicate that “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    #157111. Industry News: The Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4391 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: The Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that hoping to discover some of the best places to go in Europe in 2027?
    • We’ve asked our expert contributors from all around the globe to nominate the spots that are on the up—the places that are on their radar thanks to a flock of hotel openings, major cultural moments, talk of newly introduced flight routes, or concerted conservation efforts taking root.
    • From untamed wilderness in the Albanian Alps to the world’s oldest art fair (celebrating a big birthday in 2027) in Cologne, off to everyone’s latest favorite coastal coolcation destination in Denmark, this is our guide to the latest and greatest in Europe in 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that hoping to discover some of the best places to go in Europe in 2027? No wonder: 2026 was a bumper year for European travel, from the Winter Olympics fueling a surging obsession with the Dolomites to the total solar eclipse bringing hoards of umbraphiles to the Balearic Islands, and celebrity weddings adding to an ever-growing love for Sicily. But as we edge closer to the end of the year, there are a few clear-cut destinations we’re most looking forward to visiting (and recommending to you, our fellow travelers) for the 12 months to come.

    We’ve asked our expert contributors from all around the globe to nominate the spots that are on the up—the places that are on their radar thanks to a flock of hotel openings, major cultural moments, talk of newly introduced flight routes, or concerted conservation efforts taking root. These nominations make up the Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027—and we promise they are worthy of your precious vacation time and hard-earned spending money.

    From untamed wilderness in the Albanian Alps to the world’s oldest art fair (celebrating a big birthday in 2027) in Cologne, off to everyone’s latest favorite coastal coolcation destination in Denmark, this is our guide to the latest and greatest in Europe in 2027. Happy travels. —Olivia Morelli.

    This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

    Go for: untamed wilderness and peaceful pockets.

    The Albanian Alp's village of Theth is a patch of pastoral living—and fantastic hiking trails.

    Local bed-and-breakfasts and guesthouses welcome trekkers, who do both day treks and through hikes connecting small towns.

    As Albania’s allure continues to grow, travelers flock to the Adriatic beaches of the south. But in the northern alpine region, the scenery offers a different type of drama—jagged snow-dipped peaks, turquoise rivers, hut-to-hut hiking—and in place of shiny seaside hotels, Albanian-owned wooden B&Bs welcome alpinists for home-cooked meals after long, satisfying days on the many surrounding trails. This area was largely isolated during the communist era, given its strategic location along the borders with Montenegro and Kosovo, which means that it has been slower to open its arms to the world (that’s also why you’ll stumble into countless abandoned bunkers from this period on your hike). The feeling here is that you can still show up to a guesthouse without a reservation, you can still camp wherever you find a spot, and, yet, there is also the sense that if you aren’t seeing this place now, or within the next couple years, you’ll miss the precious moment when it still feels like a secret to be let in on.

    Industry observers note that start your trip in the charming city of Shköder, known as the gateway to the Alps, where bikepackers cycle through the city, and restaurant patios spill over with guests enjoying glasses of Albanian wine. From there, many travelers proposal stops in the villages of Theth and Valbona (a stunningly scenic one-day through-hike links the two of them), or embark on ambitious multi-day journeys on routes like the Peak of the Balkans, which traces a two-week-long loop crossing into Kosovo and Montenegro. Infrastructure improvements have made roads and trails to access this region better in recent years, with much more where that came from. What was once only known by residents and those who purchased their paper guides now exists online, meaning it is also possible to base yourself in, say, the Eden-like Valbona Valley, and embark on a upcoming route each day. Increasingly, there are elevated places to stay that preserve the soul of this place, opening in a slow trickle like Valbona Resort and Spa (2024) and SeSam Villas in Theth (2025). There may be folklore calling these the Accursed Mountains, but only because they are so vast and dramatic that their geography has historically kept intruders out. For hikers, that means a literal playground, with Albanian hosts leading the way. —Megan Spurrell.

    Go for: the next World Expo centered on play, and a booming hotel scene to match.

    Belgrade is set to host the World Expo in summer 2027, and a flock of new hotels will be ready to receive the travelers it is sure to bring.

    Industry observers note that all the world’s coming to Belgrade next year—and, it seems, coming to play. The Balkan city will host the next edition of the World Expo, a spiritual successor to the World Fair where nations come to exchange their latest and greatest cultural achievements and boldest ideas for the future. From May 15 to August 15, 2027, Belgrade prepares to welcome over four million visitors to explore the theme of “Play for Humanity: Sport and Music for All." Its status as a host city feels especially symbolic as the Balkans emerge as a leader in technology and innovation across Europe. To meet the occasion, the city’s hotel scene is stepping up, with 15 new openings slated to cut the ribbon by the time the program kicks off. The crown jewel in the portfolio is the Ritz-Carlton, Belgrade, which will occupy a prime spot on the Danube riverfront. Other big names to watch out for include the InterContinental Belgrade and the Swissôtel Belgrade. In total, these projects will add roughly 1,500 to 2,000 new hotel rooms to the city. The shiny, new threads go well with the old in a place as historic as the Serbian capital, which lays claim to grand sites such as the Church of St. Sava, one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world, and the Museum of Yugoslavia, which has a sprawling eight-acre park complex. —Kat Chen.

    Go for: a coveted summer destination at its sweet spot.

    A slew of luxury openings like Aman and Mandarin Oriental have arrived in Bodrum over the past few years, with NG Sign Bodrum and Bvlgari on the horizon.

    For the past few summers, the glittering Bodrum peninsula has welcomed a wave of luxury openings, transforming this once-sleepy harbor town into one of the Aegean's most coveted corners. Aman, Mandarin Oriental, and homegrown Maçakizi were early champions of the scene and remain firmly at the heart of its appeal, but a newly introduced generation of hotels, restaurants, and beach clubs has since made Bodrum one of Europe’s most sought-after summer escapes.

    It has been revealed that mayfair and Knightsbridge restaurant favorites Zuma, Bagatelle, and Novikov have all made the journey east in recent years, accompanied in 2026 by oh-so-chic arrivals from Dubai, Paris, and Marbella (Gaia, Gigi Rigolatto, and Maison Revka). Together they have helped recast Bodrum as a playground for the international jet set, bringing with them a distinctly cosmopolitan, see-and-be-seen energy.

    This summer also brought the long-awaited arrival of the adults-only hideaway Oku, the latest in the brand's collection of design-led retreats in Ibiza, Kos, and Andalusia. Throw in annual beach-club takeovers from the likes of Jacquemus and Alo, as well as boutique openings by brands like Cartier, and it seems there’s barely a name in luxury that isn’t lining up to plant its flag here.

    According to recent reports, but 2027 promises to be the sweet spot. With fewer headline-grabbing rolls out, the peninsula settles into a quieter rhythm, and openings such as Yahşi Bay’s NG Sign Bodrum, a villa hotel of sun-filled, glass-walled residences with two to six bedrooms, put privacy ahead of spectacle. It's the summer to explore Bodrum at its most relaxed. Reservations are likely to be easier to come by as last year’s hottest tables settle in for the newly introduced season and the eyes of trend followers will be trained elsewhere, leaving the regulars to do what they’ve always done: Dance as the sun sets on the wooden deck of Maçakizi, wander the meyhane-lined promenade of fishing village Gümüşlük, stopping for fresh seafood as they go; or hop between the coastline’s secluded bays, tucking into late-afternoon picnics beneath the pine trees.

    Recent findings suggest that enjoy it while it lasts. In 2028, all eyes will return to the peninsula as Bvlgari opens its sprawling hillside resort above yacht-speckled Paradise Bay, giving Europe's luxury travel crowd fresh reason to return. —Sophie Prideaux.

    Go for: Irish hospitality and spectacular sporting scenes.

    The 46th Ryder Cup will take place at Adare Manor in County Limerick.

    Designed by golf course architect Tom Fazio, Adare is nestled upon 840 acres of parkland.

    Industry observers note that home to natural wonders, ancient castles, lively pubs, and famously friendly locals, Ireland has long captivated travelers. While the well-trodden tourist trail takes in perennial favorites, 2027 will see another destination step into the spotlight. County Limerick, on the west coast, is gearing up to host one of the world’s greatest sporting events: the 46th Ryder Cup. Between September 17 and 19, the tournament will take place on the pristine fairways of the prestigious golfing estate Adare Manor. Designed by renowned golf course architect Tom Fazio, the championship course is set within 840 acres of magnificent parkland surrounding the estate’s 19th-century Neo-Gothic castle—a fairytale destination worth visiting at any time of year.

    Sources indicate that beyond golf, Limerick has a rich sporting heritage. Thomond Park, home of Munster Rugby, is one of the best-supported grounds in the world, with match days bringing a buzz to the city. Beyond the sporting calendar, there’s plenty to discover. Highlights include the 13th-century King John’s Castle, the Hunt Museum for its art collection including works by Picasso and Renoir, and Lough Gur, an idyllic lake beside Ireland’s oldest and largest stone circle. Limerick also makes an excellent base for exploring the Wild Atlantic Way. Around an hour northwest of the city, Lahinch is widely regarded as one of Ireland’s best surf beaches, while the spectacular Cliffs of Moher rank among the country’s most beloved landmarks. With world-class golf, a proud sporting heritage, fascinating history, and easy access to some of Ireland’s most spectacular scenery, Limerick is set to have its moment in 2027. —Camilla Hewitt.

    Go for: a city break that’ll stay with you long after you’ve left.

    In Cologne's Old Town, the charm is in the details, like this whale lantern outside Brauhaus Sünner im Walfisch .

    If you visit for Cologne's exuberant carnival, say as the locals say: “Morje es, wat do drus mähs!” (“Tomorrow is what you make of it!”).

    Let’s be honest: Cologne doesn’t necessarily win you over at first sight. It is not a conventionally beautiful city; rather, it is a feeling. Even locals will tell you that the city gets under your skin. Anyone who has experienced Cologne’s exuberant carnival spilling onto its streets and into its clubs and pubs is likely to fall for the city—and its people—for good. The motto for the so-called fifth season in 2027 is “morje es, wat do drus mähs!” (“tomorrow is what you make of it!”). Multiple crises or not, the people of Cologne refuse to let anything dampen their spirits.

    According to recent reports, and while folk culture is a major part of Cologne’s appeal, the city’s high culture is equally compelling. In September 2026, the opera house on Offenbachplatz finally reopened after 15 years of renovation—an occasion eagerly anticipated by many. Just 160 yards away is Kolumba, the museum designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect Peter Zumthor. Its lofty, lime-washed rooms and the gentle light filtering through the narrow gaps between walls and floor provide a quietly dramatic setting for the art—and a welcome respite from the bustle of the city. Zumthor built the museum around the ruins of the former St. Kolumba church, incorporating the Madonna in the Ruins chapel by Gottfried Böhm. The work of two exceptional architects brought together in one place: that alone is reason enough to come.

    Industry observers note that the Museum Ludwig is another perennial draw. In 2026, it recorded its highest-ever visitor numbers thanks to its exhibition devoted to the late Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama. Art, in Cologne, is very much a capital-A affair. Every autumn, the international art world descends on the city for Art Cologne, the world’s oldest contemporary art fair, which celebrates its 60th anniversary in 2027. The 200th anniversary of Beethoven’s death is being marked in equally spectacular fashion. Throughout the year, the Cologne Symphony Orchestra will welcome a stellar line-up of renowned conductors and ensembles. The musical celebrations culminate in October, when pianist Igor Levit will take on all 32 of the great composer’s piano sonatas in a single evening.

    In a recent development, the city’s famously warm and open-hearted inhabitants are just as welcoming when it comes to gastronomic newcomers. Julia Komp, who became Germany’s youngest Michelin-starred chef in 2016 at the age of 27, knows this well. Today, her restaurant Sahila is firmly at the forefront of Cologne’s culinary scene. Other top tables include the intimate 20-seat Onda on Händelstrasse; Vunky on Eigelstein, specializing in plant-based fine dining; Toki, the city’s first kaiseki restaurant; and the recently opened Kluth, whose six-course surprise menu, “et kütt wie et kütt” (“it is what it is”), takes its name from a quintessential Cologne saying. —Ilona Marx.

    Go for: rugged landscapes and cinematic coastlines.

    Sailing yacht Orient Express Corinthian's itineraries will set sail to Bonifacio, Calvi, and Saint-Florent in 2027.

    Hotel Basgi Basgi is a favorite among design lovers in Corsica—a grow that is increasingly looking to the island.

    According to recent reports, when Simon Jacquemus chose Phare de la Pietra, a 19th-century lighthouse on a rocky Corsican peninsula, as the backdrop for his Spring 2027 fashion show this summer, it was easy to see why. The designer, long inspired by the interplay of place, light, and raw emotion, described his show Le Bonheur (meaning “happiness” or “bliss”) as “a cliff that I add colors on top. An impressionist painting.”.

    Sources indicate that it's true. Corsica is a place where cinematic elegance meets rugged natural beauty. It's why the island was once named Kallisté, meaning “most beautiful,” by the ancient Greeks. Here, dramatic mountains meet wild hinterlands and fiery red rockfaces jut against turquoise waters, making for breathtaking hiking through UNESCO-listed landscapes such as the Scandola Nature Reserve.

    Recent findings suggest that the island long slipped under the radar compared with neighboring Sardinia and the French Riviera. But Jacquemus’ arrival, coupled with a flurry of recent smart hotel openings, suggests that may not be the case for much longer. Leading the charge is A Mandria di Murtoli, a 10-room retreat spread across five restored stone buildings in the Ortolo Valley, which is a little sister to epicurean Domaine de Murtoli, where farm-to-table living is the order of the day. Elsewhere, Hotel Mylos on the west coast and Basgi Basgi in the north are drawing an increasingly design-conscious crowd.

    Adding to the island’s momentum is the maiden voyage of the Orient Express Corinthian, a sailing yacht with 2027 itineraries calling at Bonifacio, Calvi, and Saint-Florent, opening up Corsica's fishing ports, medieval citadels, and spectacular coastline to a latest wave of travelers. —Ashleigh Spiliopoulou.

    Go for: a coolcation destination with Michelin status.

    Newly-opened Betty Beach brings street food and brewery offerings to the beachfront of the Danish Riviera.

    The 60-mile so-called Danish Rivera is dotted with fishing villages, seaside resorts, and beaches.

    With rising summer temperatures across Europe, the Danish Riviera has emerged as the continent's favorite coastal coolcation destination. This 60-mile coastal stretch in Northern Zealand brings travelers the aesthetic appeal and culinary credibility of Copenhagen, but in a relaxed setting of fishing villages, sandy beaches, forests, and historical seaside resorts that remain largely undiscovered by international visitors.

    Industry observers note that the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Humlebæk marks the southern end of the riviera, but many visitors staying in Copenhagen don't venture any further north to seaside towns. Many of the region's charming seaside hotels date back to the late 19th century. But a new generation of stays is rejuvenating the landscape with contemporary design. Cori in Hornbæk brings barefoot energy to a beautifully repurposed former hospital, and Hôtel de Ville in Gilleleje transforms an old town hall into an eclectic boutique spa hotel.

    Exceptional gastronomy abounds, with Michelin-starred standouts such as Jordnær, The Samuel, and Parsley Salon representing Latest Nordic Cuisine at its finest. For something more casual, recently opened Betty Beach combines beachfront dining, street food, and a brewery for sun-kissed imbibing. Denmark's first official wine route released last year in North Zealand and Odsherred, with nine wineries offering tours and tastings of cold-climate grape varietals such as Solaris and Rondo. —Amber Gibson.

    Go for: wild Austen-esque adventures and spa stays galore.

    Dartmoor's vast landscape, made of granite tors, walking paths, and moorland, brings the drama of Sense and Sensibility to life.

    Dartmoor has always lent itself to drama. Wild ponies pick their way through heather, granite tors loom out of the mist, and the ever-changing weather plays a starring role. Now it’s getting its close-up as the backdrop of Georgia Oakley’s new Sense and Sensibility adaptation in theaters in September 2026. The film was shot around Princetown, Tavistock, and Gutter Tor, and its release coincides with Dartmoor National Park’s 75th anniversary. As the Austen connection pulls focus to Dartmoor, 2027 is the year to stay a little longer and explore a little further.

    Sources indicate that it’s unusually special in the depths of winter, when the weather gets wild. Picture misty mornings walking the ancient tracks and climbing tors, and afternoons yomping across moorland in conditions that demand retreating somewhere cozy for a hot bath and a roaring fire. For a hands-on experience, book one of the free conservation days running on selected Sundays in 2027 to learn more about Dartmoor’s prehistoric archaeology, wildlife, and rare species while helping to preserve its future. Don’t miss Tavistock, the old market town on Dartmoor’s western edge. Its handsome Pannier Market is bursting with antiques and curiosities, ideal for a spot of treasure hunting. For a change of pace, visit 11th-century Buckfast Abbey, where the Benedictine monks still make their famous tonic wine to a secret recipe.

    Industry observers note that to feel like a main character in your own period drama, book a room at Boringdon Hall. This show-stopping historical hotel on the edge of the moor combines roaring fires and old-world grandeur with one of Devon’s best spas. Its Michelin-starred Àclèaf restaurant retained its star in 2026, a quietly heroic achievement in a world obsessed with shiny latest openings. There is nothing like spending the wildest part of the year getting wind-beaten on Dartmoor, then retreating for a spa treatment, proper grub, and a fire. —Zoe Cook.

    Go for: a hidden culture hotspot on the Iberian Peninsula.

    Évora, Portugal's prettiest city, is now home to the Vermelho by Christian Louboutin hotel.

    Évora's artisan traditions that helped earn the city its title as a European Capital of Culture.

    Although there’s really no need to do so—Évora is impressive in its own right—we sometimes refer to this little historic city as the Seville of Portugal. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986, its center comprises an imposing Roman temple, known as the Temple of Diana; a Gothic cathedral; the eerie Baroque Cathedral of Bones, next to the Church of St. Francis; and the Renaissance Palace of King Manuel I.

    It has been revealed that in 2027, Évora will turn even more heads as one of the European Capitals of Culture. But Portugal’s prettiest city remains, overwhelmingly, a peaceful place, where at many times of the year you can stroll around in near silence. Then there’s the food. Restaurants such as Tua Madre, A Cozinha do Paço, and Forno da Telha allow you to discover recipes deeply rooted in the land and tradition. Don’t leave without trying porco à alentejana (clams and pork stew), ensopado de borrego (lamb stew), and a variety of local soups. And bread—plenty of bread—with superb olive oil. There’s also wine, of course, produced on the herdades (traditional estates dotted throughout the Alentejo region). After so much eating, you’ll need to get out and about. Which is perhaps why we find the concept behind Évora’s status as a European Capital of Culture so charming—the motto is based on the Alentejo’s cultural way of being: vagar, or to wander. —David Moralejo.

    Fuerteventura's volcanic landscape offers a stirring contrast to its surf beaches—and a unique draw for travelers headed to the Canary Islands.

    Boutique stay Casa Montelongo is one of several design-forward gems, this one tucked away in the charming village of La Oliva.

    The second-largest and oldest of the Canary Islands, Fuerteventura is swiftly establishing itself as one of the archipelago’s leading destinations. First came Paradisus by Meliá Fuerteventura, followed more recently by Zel Fuerteventura (the lifestyle brand created by Rafael Nadal in partnership with Meliá Hotels International). Set side by side, the two resorts form the Atlantic’s first wellness hub, set within a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Their privileged location on Sotavento beach completes the experience, with stretches of white sand and crystal-clear waters synonymous with the island.

    Fuerteventura is also recognized as one of the world's best destinations for water sports, particularly windsurfing and kitesurfing. The area surrounding both hotels is home to René Egli by Meliá, a renowned water sports center. And beyond its coastline, the island continues to stand out. Charming villages such as La Oliva are home to a upcoming generation of boutique projects, including Casa Montelongo, one of the area's hidden gems. With the spectacular Corralejo Dunes, traditional Majorero cheese, and dramatic volcanic and desert landscapes contrasting with idyllic beaches, Fuerteventura is emerging as the ideal destination for travelers seeking a holiday centered on sport, wellness, relaxation, and reconnection. —Maria Ángeles Cano.

    Go for: a vibrant city finally getting its moment in the spotlight.

    Beyond Liepāja's beaches, converted historic and Soviet-era buildings are a reason to visit this cultural hub in 2027.

    Industry observers note that plenty of the most seasoned travelers have never heard of Liepāja. That’s about to change: the Baltic coastal city has been named a European Capital of Culture in 2027, bringing a year-long program of public art, performances, and festivals with an allocated $11 million in funding. Curious visitors casting their gaze towards the little-known city will discover art-nouveau architecture, an atmospheric former naval district, and one of the longest urban beaches in Northern Europe.

    It’s certainly smaller and considerably less visited than Riga, but the repurposed historic and Soviet-era spaces are strangely wonderful. Wiktorija, a former cinema dating from 1913, now operates as a multi-use cultural venue hosting everything from poetry evenings to rock concerts. Take a guided tour around Karosta, the former Tsarist and Soviet naval district, to explore the history of landmarks like the striking St. Nicholas Naval Cathedral. The Great Amber Concert Hall, meanwhile, is home to the Liepāja Symphony Orchestra, the oldest in the Baltics, which is already expanding its program ahead of 2027. Rooted firmly in the present rather than the Soviet past are businesses like MO Liepāja in Julianna's Courtyard, a cluster of restored industrial buildings along the Trade Canal now housing restaurants, bars, and creative outposts such as local surfboard maker Drtyboards. —Amber Gibson.

    Go for: a charm-packed city break, with new hotels and gorgeous coastal scenes to boot.

    Naples will host the Louis Vuitton 38th America's Cup next summer.

    Sources indicate that as for where to rest your head? Rocco Forte Hotels will open a 46-suite stay in the 16th-century Palazzo Sirignano.

    Gritty and pretty, chaotic and cultured, ancient and contemporary, Naples is one of Italy's most exhilarating cities. In 2027, the Campanian capital will host the Louis Vuitton 38th America's Cup (July 10 to 18), an event that has accelerated the regeneration of the industrial Bagnoli waterfront. Away from the waves, the hospitality scene is evolving, too. Rocco Forte Hotels will open its first Naples property, a 46-suite retreat occupying the 16th-century Palazzo Sirignano, restored by architect Michele Bönan, and complete with a rooftop pool looking out over the Bay of Naples and Mount Vesuvius.

    Sources indicate that but Naples has never needed another reason to visit, with masterpieces such as Caravaggio's The Seven Works of Mercy and Giuseppe Sanmartino's Veiled Christ, and the antiquities of its National Archaeological Museum, whose forthcoming second site, Mann II, will bring thousands of artifacts out of storage. The city’s contemporary art scene continues to evolve at the Madre Museum, which recently welcomed internationally acclaimed curator Eugenio Viola as its new director. Nearby, Pompeii and Herculaneum agricultural parks remain as compelling as ever. And then, of course, there’s the warmth and spirit of the Neapolitan people.

    In a recent development, da Attilio, Concettina ai Tre Santi, 50 Kalò, Diego Vitagliano, and Pizzaria La Notizia are practically compulsory for pizza, but there’s more to the city’s rich food scene. Donna Teresa and Mimì alla Ferrovia are among the beloved mainstays serving some of the finest traditional Neapolitan cuisine. —Jaclyn de Giorgio.

    Go for: an under-the-radar Ionian gem.

    It has been revealed that parga is the kind of Grecian destination every traveler hopes to find: easy to reach, yet seemingly under the radar. Newly introduced hotels in 2026 and 2027 add to the appeal, without blowing its cover.

    In a recent development, glittering Ionian water, pine-clad hills tumbling into a colorful harbor, and a Venetian castle above it all: Parga is undoubtedly picturesque. Yet this little corner of the Greek mainland remains surprisingly under the radar. Its old town is made for slow wandering, leisurely lunching on seafood or traditional Greek mezze at waterfront tavernas, and exploring seriously beautiful beaches such as Valtos, a gold sand bay with award-winning Blue Flag credentials. Inland, meanwhile, the Acheron River makes a heavenly setting for horseback riding, rafting, canyon walks, and swimming.

    Part of Parga’s appeal is how easy it is to reach: Tiny-but-mighty Preveza Airport is only an hour away, making this feel like a secret without the schlep. Parga Beach Resort, directly on Valtos Beach, makes a particularly excellent base. Its newly introduced beachfront suites, released in late summer 2026, sleep up to two adults and four children. A regular water taxi nips around the bay to Parga town, turning supper in that spectacular harbor into part of the adventure. The 2027 opening of Varko Bay nearby will add another high-end stay, with villas, a spa, sandy beaches, and a private marina. —Zoe Cook.

    #157110. Mother Says Delta Seated Her Toddler Separately And Told Her To Ask Other Passengers To Move

    Mother Says Delta Seated Her Toddler Separately And Told Her To Ask Other Passengers To Move

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A mother states Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats.
    • Industry observers note that in a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL).
    • She notes she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A mother states Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats. She says she had purchased Comfort+ and originally selected seats together. If her account is accurate, this was a problem for Delta to resolve before boarding, not something to leave a parent negotiating in the aisle.

    Industry observers note that in a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL). She was traveling with her husband, their 2½-year-old daughter, and their one-year-old son.

    She notes she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.

    “I explained that she’s two and cannot sit by herself. Their solution? Tell me it was my responsibility to ask other passengers to switch seats.”.

    Industry observers note that when commenters questioned whether she had purchased basic economy or failed to select seats, she clarified that she had booked Comfort+. After checking her original confirmation, she added:.

    According to recent reports, “I just looked and it was definitely Delta. I have 3 flight / time changes – I originally booked us in 15 D / 15 E / 15 F – we ended up in 15 F / 15 A / 16 A.”.

    In a recent development, this remains her account and we don’t have a way to verify the booking history or the exchange with the gate staff. She also does not clearly state how the family ultimately sat onboard.

    I have traveled extensively with my children, including when they were very young. There is a considerable difference between wanting the entire family together and needing a two-year-old beside a parent.

    It is unreasonable to ask an airline to rearrange a cabin so that every adult in a traveling party can sit together. Heidi and I can sit apart. One parent can sit with one child while the other sits elsewhere with the other child. We have done that many times.

    But a toddler needs an adult who can help with the seatbelt, food, and everything else that comes with flying at that age. The stranger assigned to the adjacent seat cannot reasonably become the person expected to provide that help.

    I see no excuse for the Delta agent. Once an agent knows a toddler has been assigned a seat away from both parents, someone needs to take responsibility for finding a workable arrangement and it should be someone in a position of authority…like the gate agent.

    I am also sympathetic to passengers who pre-select a seat and then find themselves pressured to move.

    In a recent development, A parent should not board, occupy someone else’s seat, and announce that the family needs to sit together and a passenger should not be shamed for declining an aisle-to-middle swap. There may be very good reasons that person selected that particular seat, and those reasons are not necessarily anyone else’s business.

    That is precisely why the airline should handle this.

    Industry observers note that an agent can review the seat map, identify possible swaps, and ask for volunteers. If necessary, the airline can offer an incentive rather than expect a stranger to absorb the inconvenience for free. There may also be a solution involving a different cabin, provided the family agrees and any fare difference is addressed.

    The ultimate solution to situations like these does not have to preserve every preference the family had when booking. It does need to put a young child beside a responsible adult.

    The published Delta family seating policy states:.

    “Delta strives to seat family members together upon request.”.

    It directs customers who cannot obtain seats together online or through the app to contact reservations to review the available options. That wording is less reassuring than a guarantee. Even so, I would expect the assistance to amount to more than telling a parent to start asking around once onboard.

    Sources indicate that parents should understand fare restrictions and select seats when possible, but a two-year-old’s need to sit beside a parent does not disappear because the family purchased a cheaper ticket and it becomes legally dicey to not sell basic economy tickets to young children. However, in this case it was not a basic economy ticket but a Comfort+ seat.

    Selecting seats months in advance does not mean you can stop checking them. Whenever I receive a schedule change, I review the flights and seat assignments and check again often in the week leading up to travel. Be sure to take a screenshot of your original seat assignments if they were not reflected on your ticket confirmation.

    According to recent reports, if a young child becomes separated from a parent, contact the airline promptly and explain the child’s age. If reservations cannot resolve it, arrive early and ask an airport agent…don’t agree to negotiate onboard…it’s unreasonable, even for Frontier Airlines.

    This is called “gardening” your reservation.

    According to recent reports, A mother indicates Delta assigned her toddler a separate seat and left her to ask other passengers to move, despite originally booking seats together in Comfort+. We have only her account, but the underlying expectation is reasonable: a two-year-old should sit beside a parent, and the airline should help arrange that.

    Industry observers note that other passengers deserve respect for their seat choices too. Resolving the matter before boarding protects everyone from an awkward confrontation that should never have been necessary….

    Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    Sources indicate that the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    It has been revealed that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an crucial part of it.”.

    According to recent reports, “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    According to recent reports, “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very organization that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson mentioned. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    In a recent development, myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also mentioned that Hawley’s fresh arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    According to recent reports, “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    16 Incredible Hotels in Morocco Whether You’re Looking for a Royal Riad or a Kitesurfing Sanctuary
