    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the gateway of Africa is chameleon when it comes to its cultural offering, and thus choosing the best hotels in Morocco is a varied task.
    • Right now the country is witnessing a transformation in tourism as it prepares to host the men's FIFA World Cup 2030.
    • Perched at the edge of the desert, Marrakech is improbably a garden city, its medina an intricate jigsaw of riad courtyards that reflect deeply held Islamic beliefs about water, light, and the art of living harmoniously with the natural world.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the gateway of Africa is chameleon when it comes to its cultural offering, and thus choosing the best hotels in Morocco is a varied task. Whether you’re looking for a charming riad stay in Marrakech, yearn for serenity and seclusion in the Atlas Mountains or strategy to immerse yourself in the Agafay desert, there’s so more to this colorful country than the promise of winter sun. It’s perhaps obvious, then, why Morocco has long since been favored by the fashionable jet set crowd, and has become home to so many notable hotel addresses. Some are so lavish they veer on palaces, others are romantically reimagined farmhouses or bohemian beachside boltholes.

    Right now the country is witnessing a transformation in tourism as it prepares to host the men's FIFA World Cup 2030. One of the biggest changes is the multi-million dollar rail expansion project, which will connect Kenitra with Marrakech, via Rabat and Casablanca. On the hotel front, Four Seasons is set to open a newly introduced address in Tangier, while Virgin Limited Edition aims to open a hotel near Marrakech. For the latest and greatest addresses, here is our pick of the best hotels in Morocco.

    The pool at El Fenn in Marrakech.

    Perched at the edge of the desert, Marrakech is improbably a garden city, its medina an intricate jigsaw of riad courtyards that reflect deeply held Islamic beliefs about water, light, and the art of living harmoniously with the natural world. Jnane Rumi—the Garden of Rumi—sits squarely within this tradition in the Palmeraie, Marrakech’s historic palm grove. It was designed by Tunisian-born Charles Boccara as a private home and has just 12 rooms: 7 in the mansion, 4 garden pavilions, and 1 private villa. Boccara grew up in Casablanca and graduated from the Beaux-Arts de Paris, and this mini manor house—with its arches and domes, expressive use of local materials, and elegantly ­mullioned windows that connect the house with a glorious garden of centenarian palms and pistachio trees—embodies his elegant Euro-Maghrebi style. It’s a seductive oasis that ­naturally gathers life, which is why owners Gert-Jan van den Bergh, an art-restitution lawyer, and his somatic-therapist wife, Corinne, felt compelled to transform it into a ­cultural hub, platforming contemporary Moroccan artists and designers, and curating art events and creative retreats. —Paula Hardy.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Check Availability at Priceline.

    Set between the mountains and the sea, this smart family-friendly resort and discreet spa retreat was conceived and built by King Mohammed VI as a showcase for the artisanal skills and flair that are a cornerstone of Morocco’s cultural heritage. The Royal Mansour Tamuda Bay houses more than 2,000 works of art in an astounding showcase for Moroccan craftsmanship and artisanal skills. Set on a 700-meter private beachfront along the so-called Moroccan Riviera, it sits low within a landscaped garden scented with rosemary, sage lavender, and mint. While there are some big name resorts further along the coastline including Sofitel and Ritz Carlton, this the first home-grown luxury offering and stands head and shoulders above the others for its service (all staff are trained at Royal Mansour’s own hospitality school) and obsessive attention to detail, as well as its sustainable practices. It’s also open year-round for dedicated spa-goers who come for Longevity programs of varying time frames in the largest and most professional med spa in Northern Africa. —Catherine Fairweather.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    It has been revealed that A shiny, super-sized proposition from Four Seasons, successfully incorporating beautiful Moroccan touches in the shared areas and sleek luxury in the private spaces. This would be an ideal three- or four-night stop for a spot of sightseeing and a lot of pampering as part of a wider Moroccan tour, with the city itself being a serene introduction to what is a very colorful and frenetic country. The true headliner here is the newly opened spa, which has a thorough menu and high-end treatments for every mood, with the opportunity to relax by the magnificent indoor pool afterwards. There’s an effortless blending of old and new, and a devotion to looking after the guest. Palatial, imposing, luxurious, with an impressive attention to detail, Four Seasons’ newest Moroccan property makes you feel like a modern day sultan. —Matt Charlton.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    In a recent development, three years after opening La Sultana Marrakech in 2004, the owners sought a quieter, more intimate spot to unveil their second Moroccan hotel. The result was La Sultana’s beachy sanctuary of restorative wellness, slotted between acres of flourishing farmland and a tranquil lagoon sheltered from the roaring Atlantic. Sustainable, sea-to-table dining is central to the La Sultana experience, and seafood lovers will be glad to hear that oysters are the star dish, with five oyster beds scattered across the lagoon. All rooms have their own elegant personality, and with just 12 to choose from, the precision which has gone into each design is palpable. The Treehouse Suite is a personal favorite, centred around a real eucalyptus tree which permeates through the bedroom floor and ceiling. There’s a lovely cathedral-inspired spa exclusive to guests, with pool, hot tub, sauna, and five treatment rooms, as well as a nearly 150-foot infinity pool outside, seamlessly seeping into the sea at high tide. —Layla Quaedvlieg.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    The rocky sparseness of Morocco’s Agafay desert has long attracted travelers wanting a break from the sensory explosions of Marrakech. It’s an ideal landing spot for the Habitas group, which since 2016 has been setting up its minimalist, sustainable eco-retreats in places like Mexico, Namibia, and Saudi Arabia. Their oasis among the lunar dunes eschews bells and whistles in favor of communal vibes and engagement with nature—or “luxury for the soul,” as the founders call it. They've now applied their ethos to Agafay’s 41 Berber-inspired tents and lodges. Each en suite tent—solar-powered, with eco-bathrooms—embodies stylish pared-down-ness: no minibars or TVs, just wooden floors and earthy cream and ochre tones reminiscent of the regional rock.

    According to recent reports, weekenders escaping European cities sink into poufs and Berber rugs inside the communal glass-wrapped lounge. On the semi-open dining veranda, beneath raffia lamps, they tuck into lamb slow-cooked in the underground oven before knocking back market sangrias by the open-air bar, silhouetted against the Atlas Mountains and flame-red sunsets that give way to heavenly constellations. This is what travel is about—less guilt and more meaning amid tranquillity, good conversation, and cleansing nature. —Noo Saro-Wiwa.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    With a name as reputable as Nobu on the door, good service, and an even better restaurant offering are practically scribed into the brickwork. Marrakech is the brand's first foray into Africa, and its interiors remain respectful of the location, capturing a different kind of aesthetic that sets it apart from its Mediterranean cousins. The location is one to celebrate. From here, you can walk to the medina and the souks, or arrange drivers to take you further afield via the concierge, who suggests tours to the Atlas mountains, desert picnics, and cultural experiences like camel rides. The rooftop is as beautiful as the 360-degree views it offers, and watching the sun cast ombre shades of pink and orange across the sky before it sinks behind the horizon is best accompanied by a signature cocktail or a serving of mint tea—poured from an elaborate silver-tone pot, of course. Every bedroom is a suite bedecked in mahogany wood and rich furnishings. —Sarah Leigh Bannerman.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that at the Royal Mansour Marrakech, located inside the medina, the draw is privacy—its beautifully tiled riads have their own pools dotting lush gardens that are made for afternoon strolls. The palatial resort, founded by King Mohammed VI to showcase the best of Moroccan artistry and hospitality, was built over three years by 1,200 master craftsmen. It’s a swoon-worthy showpiece of Moroccan decorative art.

    Each of the 53 individual three-story riads comprises a mini courtyard (with a canopy that automatically unfurls if rain is detected); a sumptuously appointed living room; an equally dazzling bedroom with silk-covered walls, hand-painted arched doorways, and generous MarocMaroc bath amenities; and a private rooftop terrace with a fireplace. Guests are tended to by a gracious staff, in particular a butler who appears silently through the riad’s kitchen service entry.

    Although Djemaa el Fna square is within walking distance, there’s much to keep you ensconced in this city sanctuary, including indoor and outdoor pools, a magnificent spa, and two superb restaurants, La Grande Table Marocaine and La Grande Table Française , as well as the indoor-outdoor La Table, which serves a formally presented breakfast and lunch by white-gloved staff. —Todd Plummer.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    This is where Charlie Chaplin and Churchill chose to hole up, and Hitchcock filmed The Man Who Knew Too Much. Reinvigorated by designer Jacques Garcia, it had a spectacular reopening in 2009. Retreat from the hubbub to the huge gardens, with their beekeepers, lemon trees, secret ice-cream parlor, and the loveliest pool with a palm tree in the middle. The Sunday poolside brunch—tagines, grilled fish, pizza flatbreads—is excellent for hungry children, as is eating in Le Marocain to the sounds of a traditional oud (a bit like a lute). For a riad-style stay, there are three houses on the grounds, but the rooms with views out to the Koutoubia Mosque and over the rooftops of the Red City are the ones that give you the best sense of place. Pick up neon earthenware jugs, Berber-style rugs, and baskets at New York designer Martin Raffone’s MaisonLAB in Guéliz.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    In a recent development, all kasbahs are a kind of oasis of calm behind fortified walls, and Kasbah Tamadot is one of the very finest in Morocco. Its name means “soft breeze” in the local Berber language, evoking the reprieve it offers in the shadow of the Atlas Mountains. First built over a century ago as a home for a local governor, it became part of the Virgin Limited Edition Collection in 2005. Now reopened following substantial damage from the 2023 earthquake, Tamadot is a lavish yet quirky Amazigh castle with exquisite carved doors and intimate courtyards, secret passageways, and terraces of reflecting pools strewn with rose petals.

    It's furnished with the extraordinary collections of the previous owner, a Venetian antiquarian named Luciano Tempo, which were included when Richard Branson purchased the place. Huge bronze and wooden chests that might have carried Barbarossa’s loot stand in corners. In rambling gardens, pathways meander beneath trellises of jasmine while apple trees frame the cabanas around the swimming pool. In addition to atmospheric rooms in the old kasbah, accommodations offer a step-up in luxury with 10 glamorous Berber tents in the gardens and six luxurious riads (lovely three-bedroom suites with private pools). —Stanley Stewart.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Industry observers note that integrating opulence in just the right measure is a difficult task, but this five-star hotel (once home to the king's advisor) pulls it off perfectly. After you enter the building with its cream-colored walls, you’ll find yourself in the lobby, a luminous space with nearly 40-foot ceilings. It’s the first hint that this hotel does everything in style: from the eight acres of landscaped grounds to the dramatic lamps that illuminate the corridor leading to the Crudo restaurant and the photogenic swimming pool, where you’ll lose track of time under the Mediterranean sun.

    The hotel’s 133 rooms are an amalgam of elements that celebrate the country’s craft traditions with fretwork wooden screens, mosaics, and bespoke fabrics created by local artisans. The Fairmont Tazi Palace’s massive wellness center includes 10 treatment rooms, a private spa, a solarium, a hammam you won’t want to leave, and sunny Andalusian-style gardens that lead to a secluded vitality pool. Let yourself unwind before refueling at one of the four restaurants, where ingredients are pulled from the hotel’s own orchard and kitchen garden. —Lidia González.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    It’s easy to forget what a game-changer El Fenn was when it opened two decades ago on the edge of the medina with just six jewel-toned bedrooms and a rooftop that felt like a fabulous house party. It stitched itself into the fabric of the Red City and redefined its aesthetic with color-clashing walls and lounges of thickly woven Berber and velvet fabrics, Moorish keyhole archways, and orange trees.

    Recent findings suggest that like the best hotels, it has moved—and expanded—with the times. Co-owner Vanessa Branson has gradually bought up the crumbling neighboring riads to create a wondrous labyrinth of 13 interconnected buildings, 3 pools, and 41 bedrooms in blush pinks, mustards, and acid yellows. Some have zellige tiles, others hand-stitched camel leather floors and carved wooden ceilings, all offset with pop art and bright contemporary installations.

    I recently stayed in one of the “cozy” rooms, behind an ornate cedar door. Between the hand-plastered traditional tadelakt wall, contemporary dot painting, and mother-of-pearl chandelier, it’s nearly impossible to tell old from upcoming, a result of using local artisans, natural fabrics, and upcycled furniture. Amid the rooftop’s pool, sunbeds and pops of color, the old magic of Marrakech endures. —Chloe Sachdev.

    It has been revealed that connecting with nature in Morocco's beauty spot, where you can be as active or as laid-back as you like, all while enjoying the breathtaking backdrop of the Atlas Mountains. Just 20 minutes outside the heart of Marrakech, the landscape starts to change—countless olive groves, tall leafy palms, and fragrant argan and lemon trees. The distant views of the Atlas Mountains paint the scene, but it's the grand arch at the resort’s entrance that sets the tone of sheer majesty. Step through the iconic Fairmont swinging doors and you’re greeted by towering ceilings, marble accents, plush furnishings, and an endless sense of chic glamour.

    Industry observers note that the main bar, Le Bar, dressed in a sleek black-and-gold scheme, feels like a scene straight out of a James Bond film. Jaw-dropping Moroccan chandeliers add to the extravagant spirit and five-star quality. Outside, 570 acres of lush green landscape await, showcasing Marrakech’s horticultural prowess. Home to an 18-hole golf course and a pampering spa, it’s the ultimate base for wellness seekers, romantic couples, families, and culture vultures keen to experience the crème de la crème of Marrakech’s idyllic rural scene.

    Sources indicate that this rare palm-framed fantasyland near Ouarzazate, whose name translates from Arabic as “House of Dreams,” was conjured20 years ago, from the wild imagination of a Parisian creative. Thierry Teyssier re-envisaged the 200-year-old ochre kasbah and its rammed-earth ramparts to honor its Berber heritage with authenticity, elegance, and an unrivaled romance. Spells at the hideaway are more magical than ever, with the handful of rooms in the North African castle joined by spacious suites at the edge of the Louis Benech–landscaped grounds.

    In a recent development, teyssier’s past lives as a theater actor and event planner keep him challenging traditional hospitality as a disrupter and storyteller: Every soul-stirring scene is art-directed and choreographed to enchant, with delicate, tactile interiors, seductive scents, and unexpected curios at every turn. Surrendering to Dar Ahlam’s rare rhythm is akin to participating in immersive theatre, with unprompted poolside pomegranate juices, candlelit Berber tents for secret suppers, and personally addressed hand-penned scrolls or other gifts at bedtime. Guests can explore vast desert-scapes by four-by-four, or let the staff proposal a picnic in a villager’s vegetable garden. There is no lobby, restaurant, or bar, just beautiful spaces unfettered by telephones, menus, or minibars. —Juliet Kinsman.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that royal Mansour, owned by Morocco’s royal family, can be credited as one of Marrakech’s (if not Morocco’s) finest stays: a romantic riad, where luxury is distinctly of the old-world variety. Naturally, the announcement of a second location sent the travel industry into a titter. Heads up, though: Anyone expecting a mirror image of Royal Mansour Marrakech is going to be surprised. While the level of service and luxury at the newly introduced location (in the once-home of the 1953-built El Mansour hotel) follows the first property’s lead, the experience, and especially the aesthetic, is a departure. There are 149 rooms, with three categories of suites, and several “apartment” offerings.

    There are four restaurants: The brasserie serves delicious French classics, and at the sushi bar, chefs from Japan take on the task of bringing omakase to a Moroccan audience. For Moroccan food, head up to the 23rd floor. Just before sunset, the room of mirrors and gold comes alive in the light. Stick around for delicious sweet baghrir bread, fried spinach cheese briouat, and naturally, more tajines. The views over the city aren’t bad either. —Megan Spurrell.

When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

    • I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, I boast often about being a free agent when it comes to both hotels and airlines…I’m done chasing elite status (at least top-tier elite status) because the cost/benefit analysis no longer works for me. But there are some days I wonder….

    I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement. But it’s not just that. The food has improved and service has been great..flight attendants appear happy (they have a contract after all) and the operation has also been good: my personal on-time arrival rate with United is over 90% while it hovers at around 50% for American.

    In a recent development, and sometimes after another great United flight, like my journey back to California over the weekend, I do wonder if I  am better served just getting back on the hamster wheel and putting most of my eggs in the United basket. This flight was from Chicago to Los Angeles and I just missed the upgrade to first class as a Gold…had I been Platinum, I would have scored an upgrade.

    I’m close…not that I’m projected to spend $5K in the last month of the year on United airfare…but it is conceivably within reach. And in the next month I’m flying Aer Lingus, American, Delta, JetBlue, KLM, and United….maybe even more.

    And having Premier Platinum status would certainly help with some upgrades and I’d put the PlusPoints to use….

    But then I pinch myself and think I’m actually only 2/3 there with 1/12 of the year left…and to spend all that money on United instead of flying the carriers and routings and times that work best for me (mostly in premium cabins…) just doesn’t make sense.

    According to recent reports, so I return to reality and think, no, the status just isn’t worth it and if I really need the premium cabin seat, I’ll pay for it. And the irony is that the majority of my flights this year have been in premium cabins and to reach top-tier status you have to essentially buy premium cabin fares anyway or else you will never spend enough. So what’s the point? Free baggage? Extra legroom seats for the family? I don’t find that worthwhile.

    So I guess the bottom line is that by splitting my loyalty this year I’ll make Gold on American and Gold on United (nothing on Alaska, Delta, or JetBlue, though I have flown them all) whereas I could have rather easily made Platinum on United had I been a bit more loyal to a product that I do genuinely like.

    Recent findings suggest that but no. I still think I’m making the correct choice for my circumstances.

    And yet it’s the allure of frequent flyer elite status is still somewhat enchanting….

    Industry observers note that these days, retirement can come in many different forms—and arrive at many different ages. Some may choose to spend their golden years indulging in new hobbies, sports, and skills, while others may decide to focus on spending more quality time with family or take off and travel the world.

    Sources indicate that it’s all about living life your way and celebrating your passions. But no matter when you choose to pull the career plug, everyone deserves to find a home base that can best support your newfound lifestyle. After all, not being tied down to an office or career means you can finally move to your dream city, or bop between your favorite travel destinations.

    Recent findings suggest that to help guide that decision, WalletHub has released its annual Best & Worst Places to Retire list—a ranking of 182 cities across the US (including the 150 most populated US cities, plus at least two of the most populated cities in each state) based on affordability, activities, quality of life, and healthcare. Unsurprisingly, four Florida cities made the Top 10—including claiming all top three spots—powered by the state's tax-free policies and warm weather.

    Here are the 10 best places to retire in the US, according to this year’s WalletHub study, along with supporting data we’ve pulled from the US Census Bureau, Zillow, city governments, and the demographic data firm Best Places. Whether you end up chasing sunshine or snowflakes, small towns or urban hubs, the words “retirement home” could be much more exciting than you think.

    This gallery has been updated with fresh information since its original publication date.

    It has been revealed that with dramatic rivers and bridges dotting its scenery, and a culture and food scene that is constantly reinventing itself, Pittsburgh isn’t just a place to be—it’s a place to make home. Even with all the benefits of an urban hub, housing prices are generally lower than in most of the country. Pittsburgh is also known for having some of the best hospitals in the nation, with an array of social services designed to take care of senior residents. The list of activities to do here is endless, whether it’s taking the Duquesne or Monongahela inclines to see sky-high views of the river confluences, or exploring the latest exhibits at local museums like the Carnegie Museum of Art and Andy Warhol Museum, or the quirky Randyland. And of course, the food options here are diverse and delightful, from Italian neighborhood favorite DiAnoia’s Eatery to take-out from Lucy’s Banh Mi, lovingly made and served out of a makeshift trailer.

    Population: 302,971 (median age: 34.4 years).

    In a recent development, cost of living: The median home price is $234,620, over $130,000 less than the national median. Rent is also significantly lower, with the average being $1,550.

    Recent findings suggest that income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 160 sunny days per year; average lows of 21°F in winter; average highs of 84°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Pittsburgh has 38.1 physicians per 10,000 residents, above the US average.

    According to recent reports, honestly, could there be a better place to retire? Charleston is the best of every world, starting with a burgeoning culinary scene. Among the standouts are southern staples like Miller’s All Day and Callie’s Hot Little Biscuit, seafood spots like Leon’s Oyster Shop and Hank’s Seafood Restaurant, and modern favorites Chubby Fish, Frannie and the Fox, and Bar 167. Add to that a walkable downtown (including the local open-air market hall Charleston City Market) and waterfront (with the iconic Pineapple Fountain!).

    Recent findings suggest that income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 209 sunny days per year; average lows of 39°F in winter; average highs of 90°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Charleston has 47.8 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

With a plethora of waterfront condos to call home, days can be spent touring art galleries in Flagler Village, taking cooking classes at Sistrunk Market, or birding at Hugh Taylor Birch State Park and Secret Woods Nature Center. Plus, sports fans will love the roster of teams to cheer on, like soccer and hockey—and Miami Heat and Miami Dolphins’ home stadiums are both a short drive away.

Despite falling four rankings from last year, the City of Lakes still has plenty going for it. The best part? “Minnesota nice” is a very real thing, so there’s a pretty good chance you’ll end up with a friendly neighbor.

    Population: 429,954 (median age: 33.3 years).

    Cost of living: The median home cost in Minneapolis is $328,351, which is lower than the national median. The average rent is a reasonable $1,717.

    Industry observers note that income tax on social security? Yes.

    Climate: 198 sunny days per year; average lows of 7°F in winter; average highs of 84°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Minneapolis has 33.9 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

    Industry observers note that atlanta is chock full of activities, be it museums, sports, live music, or just getting outside and taking it all in. All that and more contributes to the Georgia capital ranking 4 out of 170 in Wallethub’s activities index. One fresh attraction is the Atlanta Beltline, a greenway that's currently being built around the city, which debuted its Southside and Southeast trails this year. Travel lovers will also appreciate being near Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport—the busiest international airport in the world. And don’t forget to mix in the city’s innovative Southern food scene, with diverse highlights like Mary Mac’s Tea Room, Rina, and Botiwalla by Chai Pani.

    Population: 498,715 (median age: 34.5 years).

    Income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 217 sunny days per year; average lows of 33°F in winter; average highs of 88°F in summer.

    If city life isn’t quite how you imagined spending your golden years, Casper, Wyoming, is perfect for those seeking a Ron Swanson-style retirement. Spend your days fly-fishing, canoeing, and hiking right outside your door—not to mention day-trip access to Grand Teton and Rocky Mountain national parks. In terms of culture, there are plenty of art museums, planetariums, and historic sites to continue that sense of exploration. As an added bonus, it’s by far one of the least expensive towns on this list—WalletHub ranked it 3rd out of 182 for affordability. Another upside: 330 sunny days a year. Just be prepared for really, really hot summers—average temperatures from June to September are all in the triple digits.

We’ve already mentioned the warm weather and low taxes of Florida, but Orlando has a particular abundance of quiet communities, great restaurants, and independent stores—and its inland location means you won’t have to worry quite as much during hurricane season. (Bonus: Given Orlando’s proximity to theme parks, it’ll be easy to convince family to visit, too.).

    #157104. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s latest ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s latest ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz noted the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization proposal so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., remarked after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., remarked the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not substantial on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    According to recent reports, “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he stated. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy mentioned, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    Industry observers note that “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford stated Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Sources indicate that bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    #157103. Traveling This Thanksgiving? Here’s the Latest on Flight Delays Following Delta Outage

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1453 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Traveling This Thanksgiving? Here’s the Latest on Flight Delays Following Delta Outage

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Sunday, November 22, US travelers faced another wave of significant flight disruptions ahead of Thanksgiving.
    • This time around, the problems occurred at the nation’s busiest hub, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL), where Delta Air Lines delayed hundreds of flights due to a problem with a critical piece of technology.
    • It has been revealed that the delays sent ripple effects throughout the carrier's US network, snarling travel plans for thousands of Delta fliers heading out on Thanksgiving trips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Sunday, November 22, US travelers faced another wave of significant flight disruptions ahead of Thanksgiving.

    This time around, the problems occurred at the nation’s busiest hub, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL), where Delta Air Lines delayed hundreds of flights due to a problem with a critical piece of technology.

    It has been revealed that the delays sent ripple effects throughout the carrier's US network, snarling travel plans for thousands of Delta fliers heading out on Thanksgiving trips. While the glitch was resolved Sunday afternoon, the airline delayed 300 flights and canceled 92 flights on Monday morning, according to FlightAware. “Operations are stable today with automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations fully restored,” a Delta spokesperson told Traveler on Monday. “Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers.”.

    In a recent development, for US travelers, the timing is particularly stressful. AAA projects 5.96 million travelers will take domestic flights over the Thanksgiving holiday period. Plus, Delta’s operational difficulties came only nine days after the FAA declared a rare nationwide ground stop on November 13 that lasted more than four hours and led to multiple days of travel chaos.

    It has been revealed that while Delta’s technology issues had nothing to do with the FAA systems, both incidents have travelers questioning if their Thanksgiving travel aims will be disrupted. Here’s a look at the current situation and what travelers should know before heading to the airport this week.

    This article has been updated with newly introduced information since its original publish date.

    On Sunday morning, Delta began having complications with its weight and balance automation system at the Atlanta airport. The system’s critical equipment assesses whether aircraft are too heavy to fly before takeoff.

    In a recent development, while the system was out, Delta crews use manual backup processes to help flights depart. However, the technology outage still led to thousands of delays and hundreds of cancellations.

    According to recent reports, delta had 2,194 flight delays on November 22, which is about 64% of its schedule, according to FlightAware data. The carrier also had 274 canceled flights on Sunday. Although some of those disruptions were due to other problems, like bad weather in the Northeast, Delta stated that 70% of the flight changes were caused by the ATL equipment problems, according to CNN.

    In a recent development, the airline mentioned it had restored the system by Sunday afternoon. By Monday morning, Delta’s flight schedules across the country appeared to be getting back on track. However, as of 11 a.m. ET on Monday, the carrier had accumulated more than 300 flight delays and 92 cancellations, FlightAware showed. Now that the technology problem has been resolved, travelers can expect Delta's flight schedule to progressively return to normal but should still prepare for lingering delays through Tuesday, November 24.

    Travelers with canceled flights can ask for a full cash refund if they no longer wish to travel. The carrier doesn’t charge passengers to change their flights if they’re booked in any fare class except basic economy (although a difference in fare may apply).

    In a recent development, passengers should continue to check with Delta for the latest information on their flight status. When traveling for Thanksgiving, err on the side of caution and blueprint to arrive at the airport early: at least two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international one.

    According to recent reports, the ground stop on November 13 was due to a separate matter with air traffic control equipment outages and the telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” claims the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.”.

    On November 13, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the issues began, according to the FAA. The tech giant was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” notes an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”.

    Once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA notes that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications problems are still under investigation.

    It has been revealed that regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the issue. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy remarked in a recent interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these issues haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.”.

    Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring.

    Experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to enhancement the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” states Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of US Travel Association. The “disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.”.

    For many US airlines, the busy Thanksgiving travel season began with early departures on November 19 and is expected to last through December 1.

    In a recent development, air travel experts say that the FAA ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel plans should be minimal. As of November 16, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. Delta was also able to restore its systems on Sunday, November 22; as of Monday, flight schedules began returning to normal but Delta fliers could still encounter lingering delays early this week.

    According to recent reports, it helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this Thanksgiving compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually one of the busiest air travel days of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying.

    Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and initiative to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight.

    Operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop.

    However, Delta is still allowing passengers who were scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16 to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Customers' new departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy.

    Industry observers note that even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman of the US Travel Association. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages in the long run.

    Industry observers note that “The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman says. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.”.

    Airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby noted in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”.

    Following the ground stop, the DOT requested an additional $50.1 billion from Congress to complete its overhaul of the national air traffic control system.

    For more information on passenger rights during airline technology outages, read our full guide.

    Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series.
    • Recent findings suggest that have an idea for a livery that we should highlight?
    • Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

    Recent findings suggest that have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

    Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

    Recent findings suggest that the airline unveiled its upcoming corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

    According to recent reports, the most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

    The fuselage also received a substantial patch. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

    Sources indicate that iberia’s upcoming branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

    Recent findings suggest that the redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

    The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The latest appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

    According to recent reports, iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

    It has been revealed that the current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

    Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

    Industry observers note that looking for a new airplane model? Head over to our friends at the Midwest Model Store for a wide selection of airlines and liveries.

    #157100. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1416 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • According to recent reports, senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    In a recent development, that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    Industry observers note that “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., mentioned Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, stated, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she mentioned.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    Sources indicate that “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he mentioned. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    Industry observers note that but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., mentioned Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the fresh ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    According to recent reports, several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve mentioned many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    Recent findings suggest that that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who mentioned he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    According to recent reports, “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he stated. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    Sources indicate that “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he mentioned. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for upcoming leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    How many countries are in the Caribbean?

    In a recent development, the Caribbean is a diverse region made up of over 700 islands, islets, reefs, and cays, but not all are independent countries. In total, there are 13 sovereign nations and 17 dependent territories spread across the Caribbean Sea. The independent countries include popular destinations such as Jamaica, the Bahamas, Barbados, St. Lucia, and Trinidad and Tobago. The dependent territories—like Puerto Rico (US), Martinique (France), and the Cayman Islands (UK)—offer a mix of cultural influences and governance structures. While each island varies in size, language, and history, the entire region is united by its tropical climate, vibrant cultures, and rich mix of African, European, and Indigenous heritage.

    What is the best island to visit in the Caribbean?

    There isn’t one “best” Caribbean island—it just depends on what kind of experience you’re seeking. Families often love Jamaica for its all-inclusive resorts, kid-friendly activities, and easy flights from the US. Surfers gravitate toward Barbados and Puerto Rico, which boast consistent swells and a laid-back surf culture. Solo travelers often choose Puerto Rico or Curaçao, thanks to their safety, walkable cities, and friendly locals. For romantic getaways, St. Lucia and Antigua are top picks—think private villas, lush rainforests, and stunning beaches perfect for couples. And for multi-generational trips, the Bahamas or Turks and Caicos stand out, offering luxury accommodations, calm beaches for kids, and plenty of excursions for all ages. Each island has its own rhythm and charm, so the “best” one depends on your travel style and interests.

    When is the best time to travel to the Caribbean?

    The best time to visit the Caribbean typically falls between December and April, during the region’s dry season. This period offers warm temperatures, low humidity, and minimal rainfall—ideal conditions for beach days and outdoor adventures. However, it’s also the peak tourist season, meaning higher prices and more crowds. For travelers seeking better deals and fewer tourists, the shoulder months of May, June, and November are excellent alternatives, offering good weather with occasional rain showers. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November, and while severe storms are rare on most islands, it’s wise to stay informed about forecasts if traveling during this time.

    Which islands in the Caribbean are the most affordable?

    Jamaica and the Dominican Republic are good places to start if you're looking for budget-friendly rentals. But keep in mind that no matter which island you head to, the neighborhood and season you're traveling in matter just as much as anything else, and an exclusive beachfront address can quickly change your budget. To get the most bang for your buck, consider traveling during shoulder or off seasons, and take a look at rentals outside of the typical tourist hot spots.

    Are there any islands in the Caribbean you can visit from the US without a passport?

    According to recent reports, yes. US citizens traveling directly from the mainland can visit Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands without a passport. The US Virgin Islands include St. Thomas, St. John, and St. Croix, and travelers can also head to Puerto Rico’s offshore islands of Vieques and Culebra.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
    • Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    Sources indicate that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

    The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Industry observers note that peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Fresh York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

    In a recent development, prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    Sources indicate that the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer remarked in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    Sources indicate that the county unveiled this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    Sources indicate that according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper noted.

    The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    According to recent reports, “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S.
    • In a recent development, the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    In a recent development, the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The newly introduced office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., mentioned the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    Industry observers note that “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she remarked in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide mentioned.

    According to recent reports, the office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    Recent findings suggest that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    In a recent development, the House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide stated.
