    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The holidays always bring about a flurry of travel, but even if you find yourself hosting in your own home this year, you can always explore newly introduced frontiers by way of a good cookbook. At Traveler, the titles we swear by take us through H Mart with an expert guide at hand to break down the aisles, to Sri Lanka, where the palette of London hot spot Hoppers was formed, and to the sugar-dusted counters of Broma Bakery, where Sarah Fennel has the key to 100 desserts sure to satisfy any sweet tooth. The best cookbooks immerse you in the corner of the world they come from, and through their pages, narrative transforms into a multi-sensory experience. Just as we're placing finishing touches on our holiday menus, our editors gathered their favorite cookbooks of all time that take readers all across the map, from recent releases that have become instant classics in our households to vintage volumes that continue to stand the test of time.

    We'd love to hear about the cookbooks that take a place of pride in your kitchen on Instagram or Facebook.

    It has been revealed that I was lucky enough to taste chef Ifrah Ahmed's food at a beautiful dinner last year, so I couldn't wait to add her cookbook Soomaaliya to my shelf when it came out this spring. In Somalia, she writes, "knowledge is passed down orally," but she records the flavors and traditions of the culture in this stunning homage to Somalia's rich culinary legacy. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

    Sources indicate that when I’m working my way through a recipe or just slapping something together for the sake of a pantry clean-out, odds are that the secret ingredient that ties it all together is an item I picked up at H Mart. Perhaps it’s the splash of Shaoxing cooking wine that makes all the notes in a fried rice sing that much more, or the half-packet of Buldak sauce that brings on the much-needed heat to some peanut noodles. As a card-carrying fan of the brand, I was ecstatic when I learned H Mart co-president Stacey Kwon had committed the splendor of the Korean grocery store’s aisles to pages in a cookbook. Beyond just housing recipes (the Galbi Jjim is a dinner party show-stopper), this omnibus also lets readers in on the store’s history, the tips and tricks of navigating its inventory, and handy guides that will have you cooking like it's second nature. This volume is a boon for H Mart enthusiasts and a fantastic tool for those just beginning their journey in the kitchen. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations.

    Recent findings suggest that I love Hoppers, the dish. I love Hoppers, the homey London restaurant chain dishing out delicious Sri Lankan and southern Indian fare. So it’s a no-brainer that I love cooking from Hoppers, the cookbook. With the recipes in this book, author and restaurant owner Karan Gokani attempts to make traditional dishes like lamb kari and buriani feel approachable, all with the trademark come-join-me affability of his Instagram cooking videos. Some of these recipes are Proustian madeleines, taking me back to early-morning visits to fish markets in southern India or the many holidays spent along Sri Lanka’s southern coast, as well as to my grandmother’s dining table in Kerala. There’s a striking overlap in ingredients and flavors when it comes to Kerala and Sri Lanka, and it’s always a pleasure to get to sample that shared heritage. Now, if only I could summon a supply of the Arrack Attack cocktails from Hoppers as I cooked… —Arati Menon, global digital director.

    It has been revealed that since I’ve moved to Fresh York, I’ve known that whenever I’m looking for a taste of home, I can always head to the East Village or Williamsburg to Taiwanese-American restaurant Win Son (and its bakery off-shoots). And now with the restaurant’s cookbook, I can recreate their lu rou fan (braised pork rice) or tsang ying tou (fly’s head, a fragrant mix of pork and chives that goes over rice) for myself. I’m fortunate to have grown up with a mom who was a fantastic cook, but the magic she worked in the kitchen has always been obscure to me. She’s true to the trope of never writing any recipes down, instead relying on muscle memory and years of road-tested intuition. But with the wisdom of Ku, Brown, and Erway’s book by my side, I’ve finally been able to master my childhood dishes and resist the urge to order takeout. —K.C.

    According to recent reports, I became interested in plant-based dining once I started dating a vegan, and one of the first restaurants that opened my eyes to all the possibilities of letting go of meat was Amanda Cohen’s Dirt Candy. It’s one of my favorite restaurants in the whole city, with a seasonal tasting menu that doesn’t break the bank but still stretches your imagination by showing you the full flavor spectrum of a leek, or proving by example that yes, eggplant really does belong in a dessert. Their cookbook is an absolute joy to read through, especially since it’s part comic book! It’s as fun as it is revelatory, and it’s a showcase of how cooking is an art as well as a form of play. —K.C.

    Industry observers note that A friend gifted me Table for Two when my partner and I moved in together a few years ago. It was sweet, and the cover added some much-needed color and beauty to my kitchen counter. But its not just a pretty face—this cookbook has challenged me. From slow-cooked lamb and cinnamon stew to fluffy, peach crepes, these recipes are made to impress. You’ll find a mix of one-pan meals, specialty dinners, delicious lunches, and rich desserts. If you’re trying to win someone over, this cookbook will help you every step of the way. —M.K.

    When it comes to educational heroes, Alton Brown is on the pediment alongside Bill Nye and LeVar Burton for me. Watching his show Good Eats on Food Network was a formative ritual; he just has this infectious geekiness about him. As a sort of food mad scientist, Brown can be technical bordering on obsessive, but it’s that attention to detail that makes his methods so approachable: cooking is something you can break down to its basics and understand. This first volume is all about the fundamentals, and with it you’ll never make a bad batch of brownies or dry turkey again. —K.C.

    I stumbled upon this vintage cookbook at a secondhand bookstore, and I initially purchased it as a novelty item. I’d never seen a cookbook dedicated to an appliance before, let alone one I had never associated with “cooking” to begin with. But much like how I’d imagine Methven’s initial readership reacted in 1978, I was pleasantly shocked and excited by how versatile the microwave really is. There are recipes ranging from Scallops Au Gratin to Barbecue Ribs to Seven-Minute Brownies in this book, and I’ve gleaned many staples from its pages. It’s only right to acknowledge you’re not going to get restaurant-quality versions or true-to-form authenticity out of every dish, but if you’re wiling to adventure, this is one of the most accessible ways to do it from your own home. Sometimes when I’m at a loss for what to make and feeling sluggish, I’ll perform a little bibliomancy on this book to figure out lunch. Even if you’re just interested in this title for your coffee table, the photography is beautiful and occasionally experimental in its efforts to display the science behind the new-fangled microwave. —K.C.

    The World's 6 Largest Airbus A321neo Operators In 2026

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The single-aisle market has experienced a profound change over the past decade, with extended-range narrowbody aircraft replacing widebodies on transcontinental and regional trunk routes.
    • According to recent reports, at almost any major airport in the world, the A321neo can be found, and that is for good reason.
    • Industry observers note that this list will showcase the world's six largest operators of the A321neo, focusing on how distinct commercial models use the jet to redefine modern passenger aviation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The single-aisle market has experienced a profound change over the past decade, with extended-range narrowbody aircraft replacing widebodies on transcontinental and regional trunk routes. At the vanguard of this revolution is the ever-popular Airbus A321neo, an airframe that combines unmatched fuel efficiency with transoceanic legs reaching up to 4,000 nautical miles (7,408 kilometers).

    According to recent reports, at almost any major airport in the world, the A321neo can be found, and that is for good reason. Across the globe, mega-carriers and ultra-low-cost airlines alike have restructured their operational strategies around this versatile jet, but which airlines have built the largest fleets of this aircraft?

    Industry observers note that this list will showcase the world's six largest operators of the A321neo, focusing on how distinct commercial models use the jet to redefine modern passenger aviation. These range from European ultra-low-cost expansion to Asian mega-growth and American domestic hub dominance.

    United Airlines has emerged as a powerhouse operator of the A321neo, expanding its fleet to 80 active aircraft, per Planespotters.net, while maintaining a substantial order book of over 135 additional frames. As part of its aggressive United Next fleet modernization strategy, the carrier has leaned heavily on the A321neo to increase capacity availability on high-density domestic trunk routes and gradually replace aging narrowbody types.

    Operating primarily out of its major hubs at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), and Denver International Airport (DEN), the type connects high-traffic business and leisure markets that are vital to United's overall network. Passenger experience on United's A321neo fleet centers around a modern three-class cabin layout seating 200 passengers.

    The aircraft features 20 domestic first-class recliners at the front, alongside spacious economy seating equipped with the carrier's latest NEXT interior standards. Travelers benefit from high-resolution seatback entertainment touchscreens, Bluetooth audio connectivity for wireless headphones, and significantly larger overhead bins designed to accommodate standard roller bags on their side.

    It has been revealed that the A321neo is incredibly important for United and its future roadmap. The aircraft provides the range and payload flexibility required to service demanding transcontinental corridors between the East and West coasts. Now operating these modern narrowbodies alongside incoming A321XLRs, United has successfully optimized its single-aisle network to match the capacity and comfort expectations of modern frequent flyers.

    With a growing presence among global leaders, American Airlines operates 96 standard A321neo aircraft, backed by a robust backlog of 127 additional jets on order alongside its separate A321XLR fleet. As highlighted in recent fleet coverage by Simple Flying, these narrowbody aircraft serve as the leader for high-density domestic corridors.

    It has been revealed that they connect major hubs like Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT), and Miami International Airport (MIA). Cabin layout choices emphasize a dual-class commercial strategy tailored for domestic business and leisure travelers. American Airlines equips its standard A321neos with a 196-seat configuration.

    This layout features 20 domestic first-class recliners at the front, alongside spacious main cabin extra options providing extra legroom of up to 34 inches (86 cm). Passengers benefit from modern amenities including high-speed Wi-Fi, seatback power ports, and personal device entertainment streaming, providing consistent comfort across medium-haul domestic sectors.

    In a recent development, strategically, the introduction of these advanced narrowbodies has allowed American Airlines to retire aging mainline types and therefore optimize seat capacity on high-demand transcontinental and Caribbean routes. The aircraft deliver significant fuel burn reductions compared to older legacy jets. This fleet integration positions the carrier to seamlessly link standard domestic operations with premium-heavy long-haul missions flown by its sister A321XLR fleet.

    As the largest carrier in Asia by overall fleet volume, China Southern Airlines is the preeminent Chinese operator of the A321neo. China Southern has 100 active A321neo frames in service, forming an integral pillar of the airline's domestic and regional trunk infrastructure.

    Operating mainly out of its mega-hubs at Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport (CAN) and Beijing Daxing International Airport (PKX), the airline deploys these efficient narrowbodies to connect high-density commercial centers across mainland China. It also ventures into key Southeast Asian markets such as Bangkok and Jakarta. China Southern's A321neo fleet cabins reflect a tailored approach to regional comfort.

    On this front, it frequently uses a balanced three-class or high-density two-class layout. Standard configurations often seat approximately 195 passengers, incorporating a dedicated premium cabin section featuring four business class recliners, 24 economy comfort seats with expanded legroom, and 167 main cabin seats.

    It has been revealed that the thoughtful partitioning allows the carrier to capture high-yielding domestic business travelers as well as servicing high-volume leisure demand on trunk sectors. The integration of the A321neo has allowed China Southern to greatly improve route economics amidst intense domestic competition.

    What makes the A321neo so invaluable for China Southern is its ability to seamlessly handle multi-hour domestic and regional legs spanning up to 3,500 nautical miles (6,482 kilometers), encompassing the entirety of the major population centers in China. Ultimately, China Southern has bolstered its major hub operations with versatile narrowbody capacity, producing the operational flexibility needed to manage China's sprawling aviation network.

    The largest A321neo operator in North America is Delta Air Lines, which operates a robust fleet approaching 111 active aircraft supported by nearly 90 firm future orders. As a cornerstone of Delta's long-term narrowbody renewal program, the A321neo operates high-density domestic trunk routes.

    It connects major hubs like Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport (MSP), and Boston Logan International Airport (BOS). Delta's A321neo fleet is notable for its innovative cabin configurations, including a premium-heavy subfleet layout tailored for high-yielding markets.

    According to recent reports, while standard layouts feature 20 first-class recliners, 60 Comfort+ extra-legroom seats, and 114 main cabin seats, newly updated configurations incorporate an expansive 44-seat Delta First cabin. This high-premium arrangement dedicates roughly 60% of the aircraft to premium seating, meeting robust corporate demand as well as satisfying exceptional passenger load factors across competitive domestic routes.

    Passenger comfort across the fleet is enhanced by comprehensive modern amenities, including seatback entertainment screens, in-seat power outlets, and high-speed in-flight connectivity. Powered by Pratt & Whitney GTF engines, the aircraft combines industry-leading fuel efficiency with a quiet, spacious cabin environment. Delta has positioned its A321neo fleet as a benchmark for premium narrowbody operations in modern commercial aviation.

    Recent findings suggest that india's largest airline, IndiGo, comes in at a close second globally in A321neo operations, with fleet counts hovering around 181 aircraft in service. Operating in one of the world's fastest-growing aviation markets, the carrier has turned to the narrowbody's efficiency to connect high-density domestic city pairs across the Indian subcontinent.

    Industry observers note that simultaneously, it has extended its international reach into the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia. IndiGo's relentless domestic expansion has been in part due to its high aircraft utilization rates, often turning planes around in under 30 minutes at busy hubs. What truly distinguishes IndiGo's position in the global A321neo landscape is its monumental order book.

    Sources indicate that the airline has hundreds of additional A321neos and long-range A321XLRs slated for delivery over the coming decade, pushing its ultimate commitment toward more than 600 aircraft of the type. As such, IndiGo is widely projected to surpass Wizz Air as the world's absolute largest operator of the airframe, as noted by The Hindu.

    The massive influx of narrowbody capacity is fundamental to the airline's long-term growth strategy, allowing it to up-gauge high-demand trunk routes and significantly lower operating costs per available seat-mile. To support its high-frequency regional network, IndiGo equips its A321neos in dense single-class configurations optimized for maximum passenger capacity and operational turnaround speed.

    According to recent reports, topping the global leaderboards as the largest operator of the A321neo is Wizz Air, the Hungarian ultra-low-cost carrier that has staked its entire aggressive expansion strategy on the type. Wizz Air has 185 active A321neo frames in service across its operating subsidiaries, including Wizz Air Hungary, Wizz Air Malta, and Wizz Air UK.

    It is supported by a colossal backlog designed to phase out older ceo variants. Operating from key bases across Central and Eastern Europe, the airline uses the aircraft's exceptional fuel economy to open many point-to-point leisure routes spanning across Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa.

    Wizz Air configures its high-density A321neos in a single-class layout accommodating 239 passengers, per Seat Maps, which is designed to maximize seat-mile cost efficiency. The ultra-dense seating arrangement features a functional pitch of approximately 28 to 29 inches (71 to 74 cm) alongside 18-inch (46 cm) wide seats.

    This enables the carrier to offer highly competitive fares while maintaining strong profitability on high-density sun and city-break corridors. Like many other ultra-low-cost airlines, Wizz Air has standardized its cockpit and cabin operations around the A321neo, and in doing so, has cemented its status as the premier European champion of Airbus narrowbody technology.

    Furthermore, the carrier is actively modernizing its onboard product to enhance passenger comfort in a way that does not sacrifice unit economics. Wizz Air has introduced updated lightweight seating partnerships with manufacturer Geven, alongside modern LED ambient lighting and advanced cabin features across incoming deliveries.

    Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.
    • Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

    Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

    “It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries mentioned at a press conference following the election.

    While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

    It has been revealed that “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

    Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

    “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

    Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

    “This is the beginning of a upcoming bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

    Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the fresh majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

    According to recent reports, at his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

    In a recent development, “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

    “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

    Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had remarked they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

    Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

    Jeffries stated Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

    He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

    “House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

    A problem with one of Delta’s weight-and-balance systems delayed hundreds of flights Sunday, with backups most acute at the nation’s busiest airport.

    According to FlightAware, Delta delayed over 2,100 flights Sunday and canceled 274.

    Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport was the hardest hit, with about 700 flights delayed, though not all were Delta connections.

    Delta remarked in a statement that its employees were using manual workarounds for baggage processing. It also said it would rebook customers on the next available flight and provide meals and hotel rooms where needed.

    In a recent development, the FAA stated on X that the problem was specific to Delta and had nothing to do with the agency’s air traffic control system, which crashed on Nov. 13.

    Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information. https://t.co/q4Fc59VMYg.

    The outage was resolved Sunday afternoon.

    As of Monday morning, Delta’s delay rate was down to 6%.

    Recent findings suggest that while resolved fairly quickly, the system failure could hardly have come at a worse time. Millions of Americans are flying this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, and there are concerns that technology outages could again snarl air traffic during the busiest time of the year. The single busiest day for air travel is expected to be Sunday, Nov. 29, after Thanksgiving.

    Southwest Airlines' New 6-Hour Alaska Route Is Flopping: Here's Why

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest Airlines has not flown to Alaska for long.
    • It has been revealed that many routes take time to develop, while some perform worse than anticipated despite strong enough expectations.
    • Recent findings suggest that it is vital to note that data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT) is at the moment only available until the end of August 2026, although that was only half-a-month before the first season's flights from Las Vegas and Anchorage ended.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines has not flown to Alaska for long. The increasingly evolving hybrid operator's first service to the Last Frontier was on May 15, 2026. Two routes were available from the get-go, with flights from Las Vegas and Denver, both of which are major cities for Southwest.

    It has been revealed that many routes take time to develop, while some perform worse than anticipated despite strong enough expectations. An airline will often be able to tell how well a new link will do within the first couple of days of tickets going on sale. Initial data for Southwest's two markets suggests that one, in particular, might not be doing particularly well.

    Recent findings suggest that it is vital to note that data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT) is at the moment only available until the end of August 2026, although that was only half-a-month before the first season's flights from Las Vegas and Anchorage ended. As it does not consider the full season, it is not fully comprehensive and is, therefore, perhaps somewhat unfair, especially given Alaska is a brand-fresh state for the airline. Treat it for what it is: a simple snapshot of initial performance.

    Covering 2,002 nautical miles (3,708 km) each way, Southwest ran daily between Las Vegas and Anchorage in the first season. The DOT shows that 26,097 round-trip passengers were transported between May and August. However, the load factor was only 68.7%. That was over ten percentage points lower than the carrier's average load at Las Vegas in the same period.

    Southwest's Overall Las Vegas Load.

    In a recent development, this is just one part of the pie. What about fares? Cirium's Route Grader Report is right now only available until June 2026, so data provides even less of a view. In the first month-and-a-half of life, this fresh route had an average fare that was 17% higher than the airline's overall network from Las Vegas, but the distance was virtually double the length.

    When this imbalance is considered, the upcoming route to Alaska had distance-adjusted total revenue per available seat mile of 9.23 US cents, which was by far Southwest's worst result from Sin City. More than just this, it was the airline's fourth-lowest result across its entire network.

    In a recent development, despite only limited initial data, the DOT indicates that just under a quarter of Southwest's traffic only flew between Las Vegas and Anchorage. They did not fly elsewhere. Despite the carrier's daily service and 'relatively' low fares, it only captured 11% of the local market. In contrast, Alaska Airlines had 79% of it.

    Southwest was massively reliant on those who connected to another flight at Nevada's busiest airport. The overnight service from Anchorage, leaving just before midnight and arriving at about 6:00 AM, is designed for that transfer traffic. Despite this and Southwest's considerable network from Sin City, the early overall load was not good (68.7%).

    The low result was perhaps influenced by launching two routes to Alaska simultaneously, both of which have a similar schedule and both of which focus on connectivity. Analysis reveals that the top ten markets from Anchorage via Las Vegas were Dallas Love, Phoenix, Austin, San Antonio, Sacramento, Salt Lake City, San Diego, Orlando, Ontario, and Albuquerque.

    In a recent development, in 2026, Southwest operated nonstop between May 15 and September 14, with 123 round-trip flights available. In 2027, the first departure of the season will now be on June 3, three weeks later. The final service of the year will be on September 13. In total, 103 movements will exist, down by 16% year-over-year.

    What is more notable is that the equipment has changed, although it is possible that it'll change again. For now, at least, the 175-seat 737 MAX 8 has been replaced by the 137-seat 737-700, contributing to a 34% reduction in seats for sale. Perhaps the MAX 7 will take over. The downgauge means that 14,000+ seats have been removed. Clearly, Southwest is taking substantial action to achieve stronger fare, yield, and load factor performance next year.

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    According to recent reports, trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    In a recent development, the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, remarked Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    According to recent reports, “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he noted. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    It has been revealed that still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin?     • Lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization.
    • Industry observers note that unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great.
    • Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization. 2026 was supposed to be an exciting turnaround year for Lufthansa, as it’s even the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

    Industry observers note that unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great. Earlier this year, the carrier dealt with massive labor problems, and back-to-back-to-back strikes. Just a few months ago, the company’s senior management claimed it wanted to turn over a fresh leaf with labor relations, and stop fighting with employees, so that it could find long term solutions.

    How is that working out? Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation. In other words, it’s just another day at Lufthansa!

    Lufthansa and its pilots have been in negotiations for quite some time over the future of the organization. As you’d expect, broadly speaking, negotiations revolve around pay and future flying opportunities. As you’d expect at any airline, employees want as much flying as possible, and as big of a fleet as possible, since that’s what maximizes their compensation.

    The issue with Lufthansa Group management is that the tech giant’s solution to everything is to simply create latest, low cost subsidiaries. And if Lufthansa Group management doesn’t like the terms with its subsidiaries, then it just shuts down the subsidiaries and creates new ones.

    In a recent development, so that brings us to the current concern. Essentially, Lufthansa’s problem is that the airline doesn’t make money on short haul flights, given high costs and intense competition. So we’ve seen the carrier increasingly outsourcing this flying to Lufthansa City Airlines, a subsidiary with lower operating costs, operating the same kinds of planes as you’ll see in the mainline fleet.

    Sources indicate that lufthansa is asking its pilots to accept wage freezes, and is promising a certain level of career development opportunities. Pilots aren’t happy with what’s being proposed, so what’s Lufthansa’s solution?

    Management is reportedly proposing a fresh blueprint to the supervisory board, which would see the core Lufthansa brand massively reduce its regional flying, and largely outsource this to lower cost operations, like Lufthansa City Airlines. The idea would be to make Lufthansa primarily a long haul airline, and then have much of the short haul flying be operated by a subsidiary.

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa’s mainline fleet currently consists of 260+ planes, with another 120+ planes on order. One proposal would see the mainline fleet reduced to 100 long haul aircraft and 100 short haul aircraft, with other planes being assigned to Lufthansa City Airlines.

    One radical proposal could even see Lufthansa exclusively have a long haul fleet and ditch short haul flying, though it’s noted that this isn’t the most likely scenario, and it could take several years for something like that to be implemented.

    Keep in mind that going back to 2017, Lufthansa had guaranteed pilots a minimum fleet size of 325 aircraft, but it terminated that agreement at the end of 2021. So it’s really hard for employees to trust any promises by management, when they can just be terminated.

    According to recent reports, there’s no denying that labor relations can be incredibly challenging, and that the economics of intra-Europe flying are also tough, when you have competitors like Ryanair, though Lufthansa doesn’t face nearly as much competition on that front as other carriers. Then again, Frankfurt (FRA) and Munich (MUC) aren’t exactly massively leisure destinations either.

    Most airline employees want their tech giant to succeed, and just want to be compensated fairly. Admittedly economics don’t always align. But what I find incredibly toxic is the approach taken by Lufthansa management. Let’s compare it to a marriage (which I think is a fair way to view the relationship between management and employees, since they’re “stuck” with one another).

    According to recent reports, lufthansa’s approach is to constantly threaten employees by saying that “if you don’t do what we want, we’ll just get rid of you.” That’s simply not a good faith way to approach things. Why would Lufthansa employees trust management, when they’ve repeatedly torn up contracts, and shown employees they simply don’t care? It would be like threatening to leave your spouse every time you have an problem, rather than trying to find a solution.

    Nothing against Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr personally, but I don’t understand how the board thinks he’s the best person for the job. Where’s the accountability for the endless management mistakes that have horribly impacted Lufthansa’s bottom line? Lufthansa’s employees are paying the price for the lack of success that comes as a result of all of Lufthansa’s errors, from the botched Allegris rollout, to Lufthansa’s very bad luck with new aircraft orders.

    Recent findings suggest that and before anyone indicates “oh, but the unions,” contrast what has happened at Lufthansa Group to what has happened at Air France-KLM, under the leadership of Ben Smith. Smith has now been CEO at Air France for over eight years, and there hasn’t been a single strike under his leadership. Under the previous Air France-KLM CEO, there were endless strikes, and the situation got so bad that senior executives were being chased up a fence and having their clothes ripped off.

    It has been revealed that this shows that good labor relations absolutely can happen, balancing the needs of employees and the company. But it requires showing employees that you actually care about the company and their future. What was one of Smith’s first orders of business when he took the job at Air France-KLM? He eliminated Joon, the low cost carrier at the airline that was supposed to basically be a labor arbitrage opportunity. That was a way to show employees how much he respected them, and that he wanted a fair agreement, rather than one that would undermine them.

    Meanwhile Spohr’s solution to literally everything is to just threaten to start upcoming subsidiaries or shut down existing subsidiaries. The irony is that Spohr started his career as a pilot, so you’d think he’d have respect for employees, having been on the other side. But clearly once he became senior management, his love for aviation turned into disdain for employees.

    Sources indicate that A few months ago, Lufthansa management claimed it wanted to turn over a upcoming leaf when it comes to labor relations. That didn’t last long, because now the airline is back to its “do what we say or we’ll create a new subsidiary” approach.

    Sources indicate that I don’t have a strong opinion on the exact negotiations as such. Obviously it’s a tough time for aviation, and intra-Europe flying is challenging. But if you ask me, the toxicity that has been created by Lufthansa management due to the lack of good faith negotiations just can’t be undone.

    Sources indicate that if your only solution to everything is “oh, we’ll create a new subsidiary,” and if that doesn’t work, maybe it’s time for a new strategy. The fact that American CEO Robert Isom and Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr still have their jobs are two of the industry’s greatest mysteries.

    What do you make of Lufthansa’s latest threat to employees?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1594 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Billion-Dollar Companies Behind Half Of The World's Commercial Aircraft

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology.
    • He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair.
    • A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

    He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

    A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

    While household names such as United Airlines and Lufthansa dominate the skies in terms of fleet count, there are many companies in existence that have similarly sized fleets that do not carry passengers or cargo, nor do they operate charter missions. These companies never sell a ticket, operate a route, or pursue significant branding campaigns.

    Recent findings suggest that some of these firms control fleets worth tens of billions of dollars, and one owns more aircraft than many of the airlines the public recognizes. The airline industry is composed primarily of two main financial systems: ownership and lease.

    Many companies such as Delta Air Lines are known for owning a high percentage of their fleet, notably their older Boeing 717 or Boeing 767 fleets. However, the majority of airlines lease a portion of their jets, as many aircraft with long order backlogs at the manufacturer itself can be hard to obtain. Leasing is a common way to bypass delivery delays.

    Industry observers note that most people assume airlines buy the aircraft they fly. Increasingly, that is not the case. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), leasing now accounts for more than half of the world's commercial fleet, making aircraft leasing one of the most notable yet least visible sectors in aviation.

    Rather than purchasing aircraft outright, many airlines rent them under long-term agreements from specialized leasing companies. The scale of those firms is difficult to appreciate until their fleets are examined. AerCap, the world's largest aircraft lessor, reported owning 1,501 aircraft and managing another 148 at the end of 2025, with an additional 283 aircraft on order.

    Those figures make AerCap a larger aircraft owner than many of the world's biggest airlines. Meanwhile, competitors such as SMBC Aviation Capital, Avolon, BOC Aviation, and Air Lease Corporation collectively control thousands more aircraft worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

    Sources indicate that however, ownership and operation are not the same thing. If airlines do not own many of the aircraft they fly, why would they willingly hand that responsibility to someone else? While there are many sides to the discussion, the answer relates to the complexities of operating an airplane to begin with, which is far more involved than car or boat ownership, for example.

    Sources indicate that A upcoming Boeing 787-9 carries a list price exceeding $300 million, while even narrowbody aircraft represent investments worth tens of millions of dollars each. Purchasing hundreds of aircraft outright would require enormous amounts of capital that airlines often prefer to dedicate elsewhere. Dry leasing is the most common and most cost-effective way to accomplish this cost benefit.

    Sources indicate that aircraft leasing allows airlines to expand fleets without making the full upfront purchase themselves. Instead, leasing firms acquire aircraft from manufacturers such as Boeing and Airbus and lease them to airlines over periods that frequently range from six to twelve years. Airlines gain access to modern aircraft while preserving cash and reducing financial risk.

    Aircraft Owned/Managed (2025-2026).

    United Mainline + Regional Fleet.

    Hundreds of owned and investor-serviced aircraft.

    Hundreds of owned aircraft and major order book.

    While having direct operating authority of 1,066 aircraft, United Airlines' fleet also includes a subsection of leased aircraft, according to the SEC. This figure comprises 958 owned and 108 leased, at the end of 2025. This number is significantly less than AerCap's total number of active leases, which, on paper, causes AerCap to resemble a major international airline.

    Sources indicate that in practice, passengers rarely notice that a different company owns the aircraft they are flying on. Under a dry lease, the lessor provides the aircraft while the airline supplies its own pilots, maintenance program, insurance, and operating certificates. To passengers, the aircraft appears no different from any other jet in the airline's fleet.

    One recent example comes from Avolon's reported October 2025 sale-and-leaseback agreement with TAAG Angola Airlines involving 787-9 aircraft. In that arrangement, the aircraft are operated by TAAG, but ownership remains with the leasing company. Similar transactions occur throughout the industry and frequently involve newly introduced aircraft deliveries from Boeing and Airbus. An aircraft may spend its entire operational life flying for airlines that never technically own it.

    A wet lease is an entirely different form of leasing, provided by companies like Heston Airlines, Hi Fly, or Wamos Air. The aircraft is frequently in the livery of the lessor, although not always. Further, the in-flight service, cabin crew, and standards are all those of the lessor organization. Wet leases generally have a higher cost than dry leases, and are generally shorter in term.

    Recent findings suggest that the influence of lessors extends far beyond simple ownership. Because companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital place enormous aircraft orders, they have become some of Boeing's and Airbus' most key customers. Lessors routinely order aircraft years before identifying the airlines that will eventually operate them.

    It has been revealed that this purchasing power became especially significant during recent supply chain constraints. CAPA reports that aircraft shortages and production delays have strengthened lessors' market positions by increasing aircraft values and lease rates. Airlines seeking growth often cannot wait years for new direct deliveries, making leased aircraft one of the few available solutions.

    Recent findings suggest that the result is that lessors frequently influence what aircraft manufacturers build, how quickly airlines can expand, and even which carriers gain access to modern fleets. A major leasing company may place an order measured in hundreds of aircraft, a scale that rivals the purchasing power of many national airlines.

    In a recent development, orders placed by airlines themselves to manufacturers such as Boeing or Airbus are typically more noteworthy. They represent a larger upfront financial commitment and a known destination for production aircraft. Orders placed by lessors are less noteworthy, but still significant from an operational standpoint.

    While the end user of the aircraft is not known when, for example, AerCap placed an order for 100 Airbus jets, such an order boosts the inventory of a lessor. This not only provides options for customers, but an entirely different, and at times, more accessible way of expanding a fleet.

    In a recent development, the growing importance of lessors is increasingly tied to aircraft scarcity. Airbus and Boeing continue to work through substantial backlogs measured in thousands of aircraft. For airlines needing capacity sooner rather than later, leasing companies often represent the fastest available path to fleet growth.

    Leasing companies also offer smaller airlines and startup carriers alike a lower barrier to entry to operation than buying an aircraft outright from the producer. AerCap provides one of the clearest examples. The organization website published an order book of 283 aircraft entering 2026 while simultaneously managing thousands of aviation assets, including engines and helicopters.

    That position effectively allows it to act as a bridge between manufacturers producing aircraft and airlines seeking them. Manufacturers in the aviation industry have the greatest amount of market control for their product. However, some of that power can be relinquished when a customer also acts as a distributor. The relationship between the manufacturer and the lessor creates an unusual balance of power.

    According to recent reports, manufacturers remain responsible for designing and producing aircraft, but the largest lessors have amassed order books so large that they have become some of Airbus' and Boeing's most crucial customers. Companies such as AerCap regularly place orders measured in the hundreds of aircraft, allowing them to negotiate from a position of strength while shaping fleet decisions across dozens of airlines simultaneously.

    The future significance of aircraft lessors will likely depend on one simple metric: access to aircraft. Airlines can only grow as quickly as new aircraft become available, and both Airbus and Boeing continue to hold order backlogs extending years into the future. Major aircraft manufacturers, while experiencing high backlogs of orders and record customer interest, can lose control of the end use of their product when lessors place massive orders.

    That reality places unusual attention on companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital. Their order books, delivery positions, and financing capabilities may determine which airlines can launch latest routes, replace aging fleets, or enter emerging markets first.

    Recent findings suggest that in an industry built around aircraft availability, the companies holding the keys to future deliveries may become as key as the carriers operating them. The next major test will come as manufacturers work through production constraints and thousands of aircraft currently sitting in order backlogs move toward delivery.

    Whether airlines continue shifting toward leased fleets or return to greater ownership could depend on how effectively Boeing and Airbus satisfy demand over the remainder of the decade. For passengers, the aircraft parked at the gate will probably continue wearing airline colors. The more interesting question is whether the real power behind those fleets increasingly belongs to companies whose names never appear on the boarding pass.

    Sources indicate that on the most basic level, that Bilt Cash earns me 1x points per dollar spent on my housing payments (without any sort of fee), plus I take advantage of the Points Accelerator feature, which earns me an extra 1x points per dollar spent up to five times per year, by redeeming $200 in Bilt Cash. In other words, this card earns me 3x points on up to $25,000 of spending per year, plus I’m being rewarded on my housing spending.

    Points with Bilt rack up really quickly, so if you spend quite a bit on credit cards, I do think this is tough to beat. And this doesn’t even account for the value of the hotel credit, as you can stack the credit card’s hotel credit with some Bilt Cash to get an even bigger discount on a hotel stay.

    As I’ve covered, changes are coming to Bilt as of 2027. While the changes are being made in the name of “simplifying” things, I’d argue that it only creates even more complexity, at least for existing members. Essentially, starting in 2027, Bilt members will earn points for their housing payment as a percentage of their card spending, in lieu of earning 4% back in Bilt Cash on all their spending.

    Industry observers note that the good news is that through December 31, 2026, you can still opt into the old system for being rewarded, and that will then be honored in 2027 and beyond. This applies both to existing cardmembers, and those who pick up the card before then, and select this as their earnings preference.

    The idea is that if you opt into this grandfathered system and have the Bilt Palladium Card:.

    Sources indicate that just as an example, I have more Bilt Cash than I can redeem (at least as someone who is scared of helicopters, and who finds Blacklane to be overpriced even with the Bilt Cash redemption options). However, the Bilt Cash I earn gets me 1x points on all my housing payments, maxed out Points Accelerator redemptions, elevated Rent Day offers, and Lyft and Walgreens redemptions, so I get $120 in credit with each business per year.

    I think the Bilt Palladium can still absolutely be worth it under the newly introduced system, where you’d be rewarded on housing payments per the below, and would also earn $600 in Bilt Cash annually (starting in 2027), but without the 4% back in the form of Bilt Cash on spending.

    So if the Bilt Palladium Card has at all been on your radar, this would definitely be the time to apply. After all, this is what will allow you to maximize value on the card in the long run.

    Bilt is making some program changes as of 2027, which are a mixed bag. From my perspective, the biggest loss is that cardmembers are by default being switched from a system where they earn points plus flexible Bilt Cash for their spending, to one where they earn points plus rewards at a certain rate toward housing payments.

    Sources indicate that at least for me, the old system is definitely better, and the good news is that through the end of 2026, you can continue to opt into the old system of earning points plus Bilt Cash for spending, and then that will be honored in 2027 and beyond. This applies not just to those who already have the card, but also those who open the card before the end of the year. So if the Bilt Palladium Card has been on your radar, I’d recommend applying in the near future.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s no denying that AI holds a lot of potential to transform how we go about our every day life, both for better or worse.
    • People are increasingly using AI for travel planning, but here’s an interesting twist on that.
    • In a recent development, an Instagram user with 1.5 million followers who promises to help people master AI has just published a video about how “ChatGPT upgraded me to first class.” Now, that’s not as exciting as it sounds on the surface.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s no denying that AI holds a lot of potential to transform how we go about our every day life, both for better or worse.

    People are increasingly using AI for travel planning, but here’s an interesting twist on that. Can AI help you find award flights and secure upgrades? It’s something I’d like to study in a bit more detail and write about in the coming weeks, but I just saw a post on Instagram that piqued my interest, so I figured it would make for a fun story. Consider this just a little teaser, for the time being.

    In a recent development, an Instagram user with 1.5 million followers who promises to help people master AI has just published a video about how “ChatGPT upgraded me to first class.” Now, that’s not as exciting as it sounds on the surface. The idea is simply that ChatGPT helped someone secure an upgrade through the standard means — it’s not like ChatGPT used his/her/their charm to sweet talk someone into an upgrade by dressing up nicely. 😉.

    Let me actually just quote the description of the video, which covers most of the content:.

    What happens when you ask ChatGPT to upgrade your flight to first class?

    I tried this on my flight in two weeks and it actually worked.

    In a recent development, go to ChatGPT and switch from Chat to Work at the top. Start a upcoming chat and give it your airline and confirmation code.

    Prompt 1:“Ask me every question you need about my credit cards, my miles, and my memberships, and map out every upgrade currency I own for this exact flight.”.

    ChatGPT shows you that you’ve been sitting on upgrade power this whole time without even knowing it.

    Prompt 2:“Now look up my exact flight, check how empty the first class cabin is, and tell me every way I can get up there, ranked from free to cheapest.”.

    Prompt 3:“Now go get me the upgrade. Use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.”.

    ChatGPT opens its own browser, logs into your airline, and actually chases that seat for you while you sit back and do nothing.

    You can watch the video for yourself below.

    A post shared by Maverick Maltin | AI & ChatGPT (@mavgpt).

    I don’t want to suggest AI isn’t useful, but I’d say that the example given is actually very poor. First of all, let’s be clear about what’s actually going on here. He had booked a business class ticket on American from Los Angeles (LAX) to London (LHR), and then upgraded to first class.

    Now, in the first place, something isn’t fully accurate here:.

    It has been revealed that okay, maybe he edited the dates, or something, which is fine, and it’s besides the point, but as a detail oriented airline nerd, I couldn’t help but notice those things. Anyway, let’s assume this is all accurate:.

    Recent findings suggest that to me, this is kind of where AI falls flat, and it isn’t the correct way to use it. The prompt was reportedly to “use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.” This is where I get confused — you’d think that AI would be able to scour reviews online, and see that American first class isn’t (well, or wasn’t) really viewed as a product that’s worth the premium.

    It has been revealed that if AI were really providing useful advice here, it would’ve recommend waitlisting with the systemwide upgrade, and otherwise recommending the guy save his 70,000 miles, and use them for something else. While there are definitely some strong use cases for AI, I think this is actually a pretty poor showing of what it can do.

    By the way, keep in mind that under United’s updated contract of carriage, using AI to help service reservations is banned, and could potentially get your ticket canceled. Whether there’s any enforcement of that remains to be seen.

    While the thought of using AI to score an upgrade might sound great, don’t count on it actually getting you the best deal. An AI whiz claims he has the secret to using AI to upgrade to first class. All AI did was use the instant upgrade offer that was available directly on American’s website, and it didn’t even encourage him to skip the upgrade due to it not being worthwhile, or waitlisting the upgrade with a systemwide upgrade, which is objectively a much better deal than 70,000 miles.

    What do you make of this AI “assistance” for a first class upgrade?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S.
    • Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest.
    • Recent findings suggest that in the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

    Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

    Recent findings suggest that in the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the New York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

    According to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

    In a recent development, WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG.

    Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency said.

    NYC Emergency Management mentioned Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

    For Upcoming York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

    In California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A latest system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

    Sources indicate that the impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor mentioned residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

    The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists stated.

    Over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

    AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.

    Air Fresh Zealand Denied All Slots For New 27-Hour Route: Here's Why

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Air Fresh Zealand has been looking to return to the UK market for some time.
    • That being said, for the upcoming summer 2027 season, the Fresh Zealand flag carrier had sought to secure slots at Heathrow.
    • In a recent development, air Newly introduced Zealand had been flying to London for several decades.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Air Fresh Zealand has been looking to return to the UK market for some time. The last time we saw its black-and-white livery was in March 2020, when it operated its final flight from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) to Auckland International Airport (AKL). Since then, passengers traveling between the UK and New Zealand have had to rely on connecting flights through hubs in the Middle East, Asia or Australia.

    That being said, for the upcoming summer 2027 season, the Fresh Zealand flag carrier had sought to secure slots at Heathrow. According to Airport Coordination Limited's (ACL) Initial Coordination Report for London Heathrow, the Star Alliance member requested 434 slots for the season. However, none of these were approved.

    In a recent development, air Newly introduced Zealand had been flying to London for several decades. The airline initially served London Gatwick Airport (LGW) from Auckland, with stops in Papeete, Tahiti, and Los Angeles. In 1994, it moved its operations to Heathrow, where it continued to fly via Los Angeles. Between 2006 and 2013, the airline also offered flights via Hong Kong.

    However, the Star Alliance member eventually decided to discontinue its London service due to low passenger numbers. It is unclear what routing it would have used had it secured the slots for summer 2027. Los Angeles appears to have been one possibility, as a spokesperson previously told Simple Flying that the airline would most likely operate the service via the US city using Boeing 777 aircraft.

    Interestingly, Air New Zealand had also applied for slots at London Gatwick for the previous summer season and was actually successful in securing them. However, the airline never launched the flights, as it was facing aircraft availability issues at the time. Up to four of its 14 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners were grounded simultaneously due to problems with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines and maintenance delays.

    Industry observers note that these aircraft have since returned to service. Nevertheless, aircraft availability remains a concern. According to ch-aviation, Air Fresh Zealand currently has nine 777-300ERs and 16 787-9s, although only 11 of the latter are in active service. The airline is also awaiting deliveries of three additional 787-9s and five 787-10s, with its outstanding Dreamliner orders expected to be fulfilled by 2028.

    It has been revealed that however, Boeing has faced difficulties increasing 787 production to its target of ten aircraft per month, partly due to supply-chain delays involving General Electric GEnx engines. These issues have affected deliveries to customers, including Air New Zealand, although planespotters.net data highlights that the airline received two Dreamliners in October 2026.

    Apart from new aircraft deliveries, the Star Alliance member is also refurbishing its existing widebody fleet. As of late October, 13 of its 14 787-9s had completed cabin upgrades, which include replacing the older inward-facing Business Premier seats with private suites, updating Economy cabins and introducing bunk-style sleeping pods on selected aircraft.

    The final Dreamliner is expected to return to service before the end of the year. The airline is also scheduled to begin refurbishing its 777 fleet in March 2027. All of which are expected to undergo the upgrades by the end of 2027, meaning aircraft will need to be temporarily withdrawn from service while the work takes place.

    The exact reason why Air New Zealand did not receive any slots has not been confirmed. However, Heathrow is one of the most slot-constrained airports in the world, and securing additional slots is difficult. According to ACL's report, airlines requested a total of 26,832 slots for summer 2027, but only 151 were allocated, just 0.6% of the requests.

    Industry observers note that xiamen Air, which recently launched a weekly service between Xiamen and Heathrow, received most of the approved slots. However, several other airlines were unsuccessful. These included Alaska Airlines, which only began flying to Heathrow from Seattle in May and requested 434 slots for next summer. Emirates also failed to secure any of the 1,920 slots it requested, while Virgin Atlantic, Delta Air Lines, Air India and Riyadh Air were denied all 1,798, 556, 1,736 and 868 slots they sought, respectively.

    We are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers as travelers boarded AS 1306 to Los Angeles. Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge. The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached. However, the Port remains committed to the safety of all of our travelers and staff and airline team. This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.

    Washington Governor Bob Ferguson was also angry, as he held a press conference about what happened, and released the following statement:.

    ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities. Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics. I’ll have more to say this afternoon.

    Meanwhile Alaska Airlines took a more toned down approach, and just expressed “concern,” releasing the following statement:.

    We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests. Alaska Airlines is required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials. We do not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible.

    There’s simply no arguing that in terms of public sentiment, the tides have turned in terms of immigration enforcement, with even Trump recently admitting “I think it might be too tough.”.

    Q: You think your deportation policy went too far?Trump: I think it might be too tough. pic.twitter.com/NKhFjZKxnd.

    No matter how you feel about deportations as such, having them go down in this way for someone who simply overstayed their visa is a step too far, in my opinion. I mean, it’s one thing if we’re talking about a violent criminal on some sort of watch list, but that’s clearly not the case here.

    Our four-year-old is at the moment at the age where he asks “why” in response to everything… and he has a lot of good questions that often make me step back and think “oh, that’s a good point.” I put myself in the situation of being on the jet bridge here as a parent, and trying to explain what was going on.

    Industry observers note that and here’s the thing — it’s one thing if these people were in uniform and identifying themselves, but when you have people who refuse to identify themselves, it’s an especially bad look. It reminds me of another incident we recently saw at Las Vegas Airport (LAS). Like, is this person being robbed in the terminal, or is this an official law enforcement operation?

    A post shared by Chris Motley (@motleymodel).

    On Saturday, an Alaska Airlines flight was delayed by a few hours after ICE agents stormed a jet bridge to arrest someone, leading to a larger fight, which also caused more arrests. It’s one thing if such a disruptive operation were targeting a violent criminal, but is this really the way that someone who overstays a visa should be apprehended?

    The Port of Seattle has expressed outrage over how this was handled, while ICE is outraged at how its “brave law enforcement” is facing increasing violence from the public.

From a historical point of view--Let us not forget that ICE is a relatively new agency. It arose from the hysteria following 9/11, and much like the supposed WMDs in Iraq were used as an excuse to attack Iraq, ICE's creation was based on a lie. The 9/11 hijackers were all properly documented, had valid visas to be in the USA, and made a point of using their real identities. Had ICE existed prior to 9/11, it would have done nothing at all to prevent the attacks. Being against ICE is not the same thing as being against all immigration enforcement. Before ICE, we had enforcement: after ICE, we will still have enforcement but it will be appropriate. From a civil rights point of view--ICE continues to violate the rights of US citizens and legal residents on a routine basis. If you approve of ICE now, you might want to consider what might happen if ICE still exists when a new president takes office. And, if you are on this forum, you likely travel elsewhere in the world.     📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
