    Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    Sources indicate that at problem is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    According to recent reports, advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly stated it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they strategy to bring up a vote next year.

    Industry observers note that senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump noted, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    According to recent reports, “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most key stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    According to recent reports, the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

    Recent findings suggest that “Across the political spectrum,” the letter remarked, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    #157043. How Much It Costs Emirates To Keep Its Airbus A380 Fleet Flying In 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1406 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    How Much It Costs Emirates To Keep Its Airbus A380 Fleet Flying In 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Emirates is pouring billions of dollars into cabin overhauls and spending tens of thousands of dollars an hour on fuel and maintenance for an Airbus A380 fleet that other airlines are retiring early.
    • It has been revealed that at the center of that commitment is Emirates President Tim Clark, whose bet on the A380 stretches well into the next decade even as replacement aircraft deliveries slip and fuel markets stay volatile.
    • Sources indicate that industry estimates based on 2026 figures, place total A380 operating costs between $40,000 and $55,000 per flight hour, depending on fuel prices and mission length.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is pouring billions of dollars into cabin overhauls and spending tens of thousands of dollars an hour on fuel and maintenance for an Airbus A380 fleet that other airlines are retiring early. The carrier does not disclose what it spends to keep each superjumbo flying, so the true price tag of sustaining the world's largest passenger airliner is still hidden behind industry estimates, unscheduled technical directives, and a sprawling refurbishment program.

    It has been revealed that at the center of that commitment is Emirates President Tim Clark, whose bet on the A380 stretches well into the next decade even as replacement aircraft deliveries slip and fuel markets stay volatile. How much does keeping the A380 fleet flying in 2026 actually cost Emirates, and what keeps the airline paying the bill?

    Sources indicate that industry estimates based on 2026 figures, place total A380 operating costs between $40,000 and $55,000 per flight hour, depending on fuel prices and mission length. According to Golden Epaulets Aviation, fuel accounts for $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour; airport and navigation fees run $5,000 to $9,000; maintenance and engineering reach $8,000 to $12,000; and crew adds $4,000 to $6,000.

    Fuel assumptions across aviation analyses vary sharply, showing how sensitive hourly burn is to crude and jet fuel pricing. While Golden Epaulets Aviation puts A380 fuel burn at $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour in 2026, estimates put it at $11,500 per hour, and energy markets have faced upward pressure since the Iran conflict began in 2026.

    For the A380, engineering and maintenance bring a massive penalty that twin-engine widebodies avoid. Separate industry estimates put A380 maintenance alone at $6,000 to $8,000 per flight hour, reflecting the extra inspections, parts, and shop visits required across four engines rather than just two.

    Emirates is committing $5 billion to overhaul the cabin interiors of 219 aircraft, which, when broken down, comprise 110 A380s and 109 777s. It is natural to see such a move as pointless with fresh-generation aircraft on the way, but delays to these new aircraft deliveries have led the airline to refresh existing widebodies, because retiring them is no longer a viable option. Originally scoped to cover 67 A380s and 53 777s, the program expanded in May 2024 by adding 43 more A380s and 28 more 777s as replacement jet timelines stretched out.

    Each A380 refurbishment comes with roughly 33,000 work hours over 21 days and more than 4,000 newly introduced parts, according to AeroTime. Across 44 months of work through April 2026, Emirates had completed 100 aircraft, 47 A380s and 53 777s, using 4.4 million work hours, with more than half of the 219-aircraft total projected to finish by December 2026.

    Sources indicate that in May, Emirates completed its first retrofit of a two-class A380, and a subsequent phase covering 60 A380s and 51 Boeing 777s began in August. When all is done, Emirates will be left with a fully refreshed fleet that meets the high demands of its most loyal customers, but keeping so many cabins out of line for three-week overhauls makes this cabin modernization a multi-year capital and hangar balancing act for the carrier.

    Of course, there are the scheduled checks and routine hourly burn, but unexpected technical mandates added sharp, unbudgeted costs to operating the A380. In October, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered turbine seal replacements on certain Engine Alliance GP7200 engines, the powerplant fitted to most Emirates A380s, after an uncontained engine failure forced an A380 to abort a takeoff.

    It has been revealed that aeroTime estimated that complying with the directive could cost up to $528,150 per affected engine, creating an immediate financial overhang whenever covered units come due for work. The reality is, however, that exact counts of affected engines across Emirates's fleet are not public, so it is important to keep in mind that the per-engine estimate highlights unit-level exposure and does not necessarily translate into a confirmed fleetwide bill.

    Structural checks also interrupted availability earlier in the year, showing that airframe aging brings its own surprise bills. In June 2026, Airbus conducted inspections on 16 A380s, 15 of those being operated by Emirates, after cracks turned up in a key wing component, which resulted in unscheduled inspection work on high-utilization widebodies.

    Spending heavily on an airframe only pays off when the jet is generating revenue, though interestingly, nearly 30 Emirates A380s sat out of service at some point in 2026 due to cabin overhauls, routine maintenance, or temporary operational changes, as reported by Arabian Gulf Business Insight. Even with that downtime, Emirates expects roughly 110 A380s to be in active service by the end of 2026, showing how much capacity the airline can still field once aircraft cycle back onto the schedule instead of leaving the entire double-decker subfleet parked.

    In a recent development, temporary schedule trims and flight reductions in 2026 show how swiftly fleet availability ripples through Emirates's network from Dubai. When widebodies step off the line for maintenance, refurbishment, or operational adjustments, planners will need to trim frequencies or reshuffle aircraft assignments because stretching every remaining superjumbo indefinitely across long-haul sectors just doesn't work in this kind of scenario.

    Every parked or temporarily sidelined A380 carries an opportunity cost alongside direct upkeep, tying up high-capacity seats during peak travel windows when demand is high. Getting those grounded frames back into rotation and keeping the active core flying reliably is central to turning high fixed and maintenance spending into ticket revenue.

    According to recent reports, it is clear today that the A380 is not something that the vast majority of airlines want, but Emirates still accepts the steep hourly burn, multi-billion-dollar cabin spending, and sudden technical bills. The reason for this is that Emirates President Tim Clark regards the Airbus A380 as "the most profitable asset in our fleet." Where other airlines have widely regarded the four-engine superjumbo as an oversized relic that is expensive to fill and costly to power, Emirates sees its high-capacity footprint as a core commercial engine when demand peaks on major trunk routes.

    No aircraft right now in production matches the A380's passenger capacity in a single airframe, which explains why Emirates intends to fly the type until roughly 2041 despite persistent four-engine cost pressure. Replacing hundreds of double-decker seats at slot-constrained airports with smaller twin-engine widebodies would mean that Emirates has to add more frequencies or leave high-demand departures with fewer seats to sell during peak periods.

    According to recent reports, even so, keeping an aging four-engine type flying toward 2041 is not a free pass from economic friction, since fuel volatility and higher maintenance intensity continually test that profitability thesis. Emirates holds on to that massive revenue-generating capacity, but something naturally has to give. That being the high per-hour costs and long-horizon airframe support, which will continue to be the defining trade-off behind Emirates's willingness to pay for the A380.

    Whether the A380 can stay as a commercial winner for Emirates through the next decade is really dependent on how fuel prices behave after the 2026 Iran conflict shock and how rapidly replacement widebody deliveries arrive. The higher-than-ever jet fuel costs hit four-engine economics harder than twin-engine competitors, while ongoing OEM delivery delays determine how long Emirates must lean on refurbished double-deckers to hold capacity across major trunk routes without losing market share at slot-constrained hubs.

    Industry observers note that december 2026 offers an immediate checkpoint on that trajectory, as Emirates aims to have more than half of its 219-aircraft cabin retrofit program completed and roughly 110 A380s in active service by year-end. Meeting those targets, all while managing unscheduled engine and airframe checks, from turbine seal directives to structural inspections, will be what highlights whether Emirates can keep its biggest revenue earner ahead of its rising upkeep as aircraft cycle through hangars.

    The question that many still have is how smoothly a replacement aircraft eventually arrives, which at the moment is considered to be the Boeing 777X, and how stubborn fuel and maintenance expenses prove over the coming years. Whatever the future holds, it ultimately will decide whether keeping the A380 flying until about 2041 stays an asset or turns into a heavier burden. For now, Emirates is betting that unmatched single-airframe scale outweighs higher per-hour and refurbishment costs, even as every shift in oil prices or delivery schedules tests the margin on that strategy.
